chapters.title: Council staff opens hearing and sets rules

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Welcome to the New York City Council hearing for the Committee on Small Business, jointly with the Subcommittee on Early Childhood Education.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: At this time, we're going to ask everyone in the room to silence all cell phones and electronic devices.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: If you wish to testify, you need to fill out an appearance card.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: If you haven't done so yet,

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Please see the sergeant at arms in the back of the room, and we'll get you signed up.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Chair, you may begin.

chapters.summary: Chair Shanel Thomas-Henry welcomes attendees to the joint hearing of the Committee on Small Business and Subcommittee on Early Childhood Education. She thanks co-chair Jennifer Gutierrez, administration representatives, and colleagues present.
chapters.title: Chair Thomas-Henry welcomes attendees and introduces joint hearing

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everyone.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: I am Councilmember Chanel Thomas-Henry, Chair of the Committee on Small Business.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Thank you for joining us for today's joint hearing between the Committee on Small Business and Subcommittee on Early Childhood Education to examine the business of child care.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: I'd like to begin by thanking my co-chair, Councilmember Jennifer Gutierrez.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: I'd like to also thank the representatives from the administration, members of the public, and my council colleagues who have joined us here today, including Councilmember Santa Suarez.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Joseph, Felder, and Brewer.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And on Zoom, we have Councilmember Maloney.

chapters.summary: Thomas-Henry frames the hearing around child care affordability and the role of small businesses as providers. She cites a 2024 SBA report that nearly all child care firms are small businesses and that child care prices grew 230% from 1990 to 2022.
chapters.title: Chair frames child care crisis and small business providers

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: The last couple of years, we've seen conversation grow significantly around child care in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: This year, the mayor, the governor, and the council have focused their efforts to examine the landscape of child care and approve its affordability and accessibility for New York City families.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Part of this examination is considering who would provide child care, and that is why today's hearing is so important.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: New York City small businesses are significant providers of child care, and ensuring that they have the resources and guidance to conduct their business is crucial to meeting the affordability needs of New York City families.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: According to a 2024 report from the U.S.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Small Business Administration, nearly all firms in the child care industry are small businesses.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: But most of the child care firms that have exited the market have been small businesses.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: The growing cost of the industry has been an overwhelming burden for small businesses, and this 2024 report further noted that the price of child care grew by 230%

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: from 1990 to 2022.

chapters.summary: Thomas-Henry describes child care small businesses as deeply community-connected but burdened by complex requirements and regulations. She argues the city must streamline the business of child care to make care affordable.
chapters.title: Chair discusses small business community ties and regulatory complexity

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Small businesses have the unique ability to be deeply connected to their

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: communities.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Many serve as unofficial community centers or were started by someone who was born and raised in the neighborhood.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Businesses can begin because of deep need to give back to the community or share a passion, but starting a small child care business takes a unique amount of work.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: There are many complex requirements that a child care business must meet, in addition to a myriad rules and regulations that all small businesses must follow in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: The cost and the complexity of starting and sustaining a child care business cannot be understated.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And we must find ways to appropriately streamline the business of child care if we truly want to make child care affordable.

chapters.summary: Thomas-Henry introduces Intro 445 from Councilmember Stevens, which would expand the Business Pathways program to creative fields, retail, and cosmetology. She notes the program currently serves NYCHA residents in food and child care and that public information is limited.
chapters.title: Chair introduces Intro 445 Business Pathways expansion

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: The committee is also hearing Introduction 445 from Councilmember Stevens, which requires the Department of Small Business Services to expand the Business Pathways program to include creative fields, retail, and cosmetology.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: The programs would assist NYCHA residents in formalizing their businesses, including via professional business education course, mentorship, and professional coaching.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Support in obtaining business licenses, guidance on business operations, marketing and financial structures, funding to complete required health and safety trainings,

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: support in completing provider applications, and help for certain businesses to secure commercial space.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: The Business Pathways Program currently empowers entrepreneurs who reside in NITRA housing to start and grow businesses in food and child care, the latter of which we plan to focus on for this hearing.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Public information about this program is limited, including who is presently responsible for running the program, and we look forward to hearing from the administration about this program and their thoughts on Council Member Stevens'bill.

chapters.summary: Thomas-Henry thanks Central Staff and her own staff for organizing the hearing. She acknowledges Councilmember Morano and turns the floor to co-chair Gutierrez.
chapters.title: Chair thanks staff and acknowledges colleagues

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: I would like to thank Tyler Walls and Rebecca Barilla from Central Staff for their work putting this hearing together, as well as my own staff, Derek Slaughter, Franklin Richards, and Sierra Smith, and everyone working

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: in the background to help make this hearing possible.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: I'd also...

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: I'd like to mention, I believe we were joined by Councilmember Moreno.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Moreno.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: He's here somewhere.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: All right, we'll find Councilmember Morano shortly.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: In the meantime, I will turn it over to my co-chair, Councilmember Gutierrez, for remarks.

chapters.summary: Councilmember Jennifer Gutierrez, chair of the Subcommittee on Early Childhood Education, welcomes attendees. She describes child care providers as caught in an impossible squeeze between high costs for families and low wages for staff.
chapters.title: Co-chair Gutierrez welcomes and describes provider squeeze

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everyone.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I'm Councilmember Gutierrez, Chair of the Subcommittee on Early Childhood Education.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: We're so excited to join the Committee on Small Business and their Chair, Councilmember Chanel Thomas-Henry, for today's oversight hearing on the business of child care.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Over the last several months, as Chair of the Subcommittee, I've had the privilege of hearing directly from families about how reliable, affordable child care plays an integral role in their lives.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Yet the people who run child care programs are caught in an impossible squeeze.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Child care providers are asked to deliver high-quality, safe, and nurturing environments on razor-thin margins.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: They are competing in a market where the service is expensive for families to buy, and the wages they can afford to pay their staff remain far too low.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: As former Treasury Secretary Janet Yellen described, the child care industry is the textbook example of a broken market.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: The majority of child care businesses are small business and are owned and operated largely by women and often women of color.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Most are working hard and following the rules to keep their child care business open, but this can often feel impossible.

chapters.summary: Gutierrez calls the child care industry a textbook broken market, noting most providers are small businesses owned by women of color. She says for-profit facilities often operate on less than 1% margins and need public funding at the true cost of care.
chapters.title: Gutierrez on broken child care market and public funding

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: National data shows that most for-profit child care facilities operate on a profit margin of less than 1%, well below the recommended healthy margin of 15% seen across most industries.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: This means if an unexpected cost pops up,

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: like a broken fridge or plumbing backups or water heater.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: failures, it can often be devastating to the financial stability of that child care program.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: This year, Mayor Mamdani and Governor Hochul made a big investment in expanding the child care system, but improving child care access for families is not just about making child care more affordable.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: The underlying infrastructure needs investment, too.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: This means increasing contracted rates for DOE child care seats and setting reimbursement rates for child care vouchers at the true cost of care.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Without sufficient public funding, child care programs will continue to struggle.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: So today we'll ask the Mayor's Office of Child Care and Early Childhood Education and the Department of Small Business Services, how are you supporting child care businesses as small businesses?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And how are you ensuring the financial viability of child care programs?

chapters.summary: Gutierrez thanks subcommittee members and staff for their work on the hearing. She turns the floor back to Chair Thomas-Henry.
chapters.title: Gutierrez thanks subcommittee and staff

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Thank you to the members of the Subcommittee on Early Childhood who've joined us today.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I also want to thank the staff, Julia Goldsmith-Pinkham, Katie Salina, Grace Amato, and Julian Lawless and Margaret.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Barnsley, as well as my own staff, Frank Hulka, Angelica Colon, and Madeline McGillibray for their work on today's hearing.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Oh, and Soleil, my legislative fellow.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I'll turn it back over to you.

chapters.title: Chair administers oath to administration panel

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember Gutierrez.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: I will now turn it over to the Committee Council to administer the oath before we hear from the mayoral administration.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Can all admin staff, admin representatives come up to the table, including Nitra?

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Do you affirm to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth before this committee and to respond honestly to council member questions?

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: You may be getting ready.

chapters.summary: Emmy Liss, Executive Director of the Mayor's Office of Child Care and Early Childhood Education, introduces herself and her colleagues from SBS and NYCHA. She acknowledges early childhood educators and advocates in the room.
chapters.title: Emmy Liss introduces herself and acknowledges providers

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair Gutierrez, Chair Thomas Henry, members of the Subcommittee on Early Childhood Education, members of the Committee on Small Business, and all other City Council members.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: My name is Emmy Liss, and I'm the Executive Director of the Mayor's Office of Child Care and Early Childhood Education.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: I'm joined today by my colleagues at the Department of Small Business Services and New York City Housing Authority.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Thank you for organizing this hearing and giving us the opportunity to testify about the business of child care.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: I would also like to acknowledge and recognize the early childhood educators and providers who have joined us for this hearing today, as well as the advocacy groups and organizations who support this critical workforce.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: We are grateful for the work you do every day in our city's early childhood programs and appreciate you being here to share your stories and experiences.

chapters.summary: Liss says universal child care is a pillar of the Mamdani administration and describes a vision of free, high-quality care for children under five. She notes the governor committed over $1.2 billion to New York City on day eight of the administration.
chapters.title: Liss outlines universal child care vision and state investment

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Universal child care is a critical pillar for the MomDani administration and a key component in making New York City more affordable for everyone to raise a family.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: This administration has been working diligently toward a city where every child under five has access to free, high-quality early care and education offered in a range of culturally competent settings with care.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: givers and educators who are trained, respected, and fairly compensated.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: On just day eight of this administration, the mayor stood with the governor as she committed over $1.2 billion to New York City to put us more firmly on a path to universal child care.

chapters.summary: Liss presents state licensing data: over 10,000 licensed child care programs in NYC, including 2,200 daycare centers, 1,500 school-age centers, 5,600 group family daycares, and 740 family daycares. She says more than half employ fewer than five people.
chapters.title: Liss presents NYC child care provider ecosystem statistics

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Here in New York City, we are lucky to have a rich ecosystem of early childhood education providers.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Many of the city's community-based child care providers have been in operation for decades or more than a century in some cases, and they have educated and cared for thousands and thousands of children.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: We appreciate that today's hearing recognizes child care providers as the small businesses that they are.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: According to state licensing data, there are more than 10,000 unique licensed child care programs in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Over 2,200 licensed daycare centers, more than 1,500 licensed school-age child care centers, close to 5,600 group family daycares, and around 740 family daycares.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Child care businesses in New York City are typically very small.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Small family child care programs may not have any staff other than the owner, and larger family child care programs may have just one or two additional staff members.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: According to data from the U.S.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Census, more than half of child care programs operating in New York City employ fewer than five people.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Just 3% of child care businesses employ more than 50.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: As small businesses, New York City's child care leaders, a majority of whom are women of color, often wear many hats.

chapters.summary: Liss says child care leaders, mostly women of color, wear many hats and face a challenging regulatory landscape. She notes over 5,000 child care workers have a child under five at home.
chapters.title: Liss on regulatory challenges and child care workers with children

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: And New York City's regulatory landscape for child care providers, while important for health and safety, can make life very challenging for our child care business owners.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Close to half of all child care providers

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Child care workers have their own children at home.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: In total, over 5,000 child care workers have a child under the age of five at home, meaning they are likely making use of early care and education themselves.

chapters.summary: Liss describes her office's mandate to make care easier to find and afford and to help providers open, operate, and sustain businesses. She outlines strategy, coordination, community engagement, and partnerships.
chapters.title: Liss describes office mandate and strategy

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: The Mayor's Office of Child Care and Early Childhood Education sees its mandate simply, to make it easier for families to find access and afford care, and to make it easier for child care providers to open, operate, and sustain their businesses.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: We do this by setting the administration's strategy to deliver on universal child care, coordinating and aligning policy and programmatic activity across agencies involved in early care and education work,

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: engaging deeply with community to ensure parent and child care provider voices are represented in policymaking, and partnering with business, philanthropy, and the nonprofit sector to accelerate innovation and impact.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Over the past 10 months, we have spent time listening to child care providers to try to better understand what they need and how the city can better support their work, which is essential to delivering on our vision of universal child care.

chapters.summary: Liss lists recent actions: a new child care center permitting portal launched in April, Child Care Provider Appreciation Month in May, and a listening tour with home-based providers. She also mentions a procurement overhaul announced in August.
chapters.title: Liss lists recent actions: permitting portal, appreciation month, listening tour

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: In April, we launched a new child care center provider permitting portal, which consolidates application requirements, simplifies communication with the health department, and provides real-time updates on application status, removing barriers that have long made it difficult for providers to open their doors.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: And we were pleased to demo that permitting portal for the council earlier this year.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: In May, Mayor Mamdani issued a proclamation declaring Child Care Provider Appreciation Month and coordinated a series of visits to child care providers across the city intended to bring more visibility to the work that our providers do every day.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Additionally, my office has partnered with Providers Organized for Power, or POP, to lead a listening tour with home-based child care programs

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: focused on fostering honest conversations with educators as part of our commitment to supporting the educators who make child care possible for working families across New York City.

chapters.summary: Liss details the August overhaul of child care procurement, including a $43 million investment to transform NYC Public Schools' Division of Early Childhood Education. The goal is to prevent contracting and payment delays.
chapters.title: Liss on procurement overhaul and $43M investment

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: In August, Mayor Ramdani and Schools Chancellor Kumar Samuels announced a comprehensive overhaul of the city's child care procurement processes to ensure providers working with New York City public schools can open their doors and to work to accelerate contract registration.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: This overhaul included a $43 million investment to transform New York City Public Schools Division of Early Childhood Education to ensure the staffing capacity necessary to implement reforms designed to prevent future contracting and payment delays.

chapters.summary: Liss discusses a provider-led steering committee designing a shared services cooperative for home-based providers. She says the co-op could reduce costs, increase revenue, and help small providers compete with larger chains.
chapters.title: Liss on shared services cooperative and insurance costs

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Our team in the mayor's office is helping to coordinate a provider-led steering committee to design a shared services cooperative for home-based providers to reduce costs, drive up revenue, and help providers build power together.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: This co-op would serve as a tool to empower our small family child care businesses to compete with larger chains that threaten the business model of our essential small business providers.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Lastly, we know that our small child care businesses face a crisis of rapidly growing costs, especially liability insurance, and they lack the negotiating leverage to resolve those.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: We believe we should use the levers of government to support our small businesses in reducing costs like these.

chapters.summary: Liss says small child care businesses face rapidly growing costs, especially liability insurance, and lack negotiating leverage. She outlines workforce strategy, budget investments including a $40 million rate increase and a $3 million emergency microgrant fund, and 2K procurement opportunities.
chapters.title: Liss on workforce strategy and budget investments

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Looking ahead,

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: The city is bringing together partners within and outside government to develop a comprehensive strategy to grow, sustain, and support the child care workforce,

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: including addressing wage disparities, rising operating costs, and the long-term investments needed to support competitive compensation and high-quality care.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: As the administration works with urgency to implement universal child care, we know that we must invest in child care operators and ensure they can sustain their businesses.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: In the past several months, we have taken some initial steps to address the financial and operational challenges facing providers and the educators who make these programs possible, though we know there is still much more work to do.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: In the executive budget, the mayor invested $40 million to increase rates for contracted early childhood providers, including a 5% rate increase for family child care providers and a 2% increase for family child care networks and center-based providers.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: The administration also launched a $3 million emergency microgrant fund to provide financial assistance to licensed home-based child care providers facing urgent challenges that threaten their ability to remain open.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: And with the city's recent announcement of where geographically we will offer 2K in fall 2027, we have opened procurement opportunities for child care providers who may wish to offer 2K services.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: There is a survey open now to existing early childhood contracted providers, which they must complete by November 9th, and a request for information for potential new partners with New York City Public Schools, which will be open until November 12th.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: I will now turn it over to my colleague.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Aris Khan, Chief of Staff at the Department of Small Business Services, who will speak to how SBS supports the critical work that our child care providers do as small businesses in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: We look forward to your questions today and your partnership in this work.

chapters.summary: Haris Khan, Chief of Staff at the Department of Small Business Services, introduces SBS's mission to unlock economic potential and create economic security. He says child care providers play a dual role as businesses and family support systems.
chapters.title: Haris Khan introduces SBS mission

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair Thomas Henry, Chair Gutierrez, and members of the New York City Council Committee on Small Business and Subcommittee on Early Childhood Education.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: My name is Haris Khan.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: I serve as Chief of Staff at the City's Department of Small Business Services, or SBS for short.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: SBS's mission is to unlock economic potential and create economic security for all New Yorkers by connecting New Yorkers to good jobs, creating stronger businesses, and building thriving neighborhoods across the five boroughs.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Small businesses are the backbone of our economy, and the city's independently owned child care providers play a dual role.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: They help sustain our economy and serve as a central support system for thousands of families.

chapters.summary: Khan describes SBS services including educational resources, commercial lease assistance, and worker cooperative support. He highlights the OPEN for Small Business Reform Agenda, which includes four child care-focused reforms.
chapters.title: Khan describes SBS services and OPEN reforms

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: SVS is committed to supporting all small businesses, including child care providers, by offering educational resources on topics such as opening a storefront business, forming a worker cooperative, securing financing, and

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: accessing free commercial lease assistance legal services.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: We're grateful for our ongoing partnership with the Mayor's Office of Child Care and Early Childhood Education and the Department of Health and Mental Hygiene in supporting these operators.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: In addition to our direct services, SPS partnered with City Hall in the development and implementation of the OPEN for Small Business Reform Agenda, which includes more than 50 reforms with four specifically focused on child care.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: These reforms

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: include expanding the child care permitting portal and upgrading the background check request portal.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: In this process, the administration gathered insights from industry leaders and direct feedback from small business operators, including a child care operators roundtable led by Deputy Mayor Julie Hsu and Executive Director Liss.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Additionally, we partner with the Office of Child Care and Early Childhood Education in our public events and webinars to help educate small businesses.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Our New York City Business Express service team also works with DOHMH to guide child care providers through the city requirements and connects them to the full suite of SBS services as needed.

chapters.summary: Khan discusses the Business Pathways program referenced in Intro 445, noting it is operated by NYCHA's REES office. He shares enrollment statistics and introduces Shana Castillo from NYCHA.
chapters.title: Khan on Business Pathways program and NYCHA colleague

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Additionally, I'd like to briefly speak on the Business Pathways program referenced in Introduction 445, sponsored by Councilmember Lthea Stevens.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: The Business Pathways program is operated by NYCHA's Office of Resident Economic Empowerment and Sustainability, REES.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: According to NYCHA,

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Since 2014, the program has enrolled 448 residents in 12 cohorts of the food business pathways to start or grow their food businesses, and 189 residents across nine cohorts of the child care business pathways

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: to start and formalize their child care business.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: We're joined today by my colleague, Shana Castillo, Vice President of Partnerships and Initiatives at NYCHA, who can answer further questions on this program.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: We're also grateful for the partnership of the New York City Council as a critical partner in all of our work, and thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: this opportunity to testify and I welcome any questions that you may have.

chapters.summary: Chair Thomas-Henry thanks the administration panel and announces that Councilmembers Morano, Riley, and Maloney have joined. She turns to Councilmember Joseph for questions.
chapters.title: Chair thanks panel and announces members present

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Thank you both for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: I'd like to announce that we found Councilmember Morano has joined us.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: We've also been joined by Councilmember Riley and Councilmember Maloney on Zoom.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: I will now turn it over to Councilmember Joseph to ask questions.

chapters.summary: Councilmember Rita Joseph asks about the roughly 5,000 family child care providers not in networks and why FCCs are paid less than CBOs for the same seat. Emmy Liss explains networks serve as intermediaries and says networks should not charge providers fees.
chapters.title: Joseph questions FCC networks and provider fees

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Chairs, for this allowing me to go before.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: So there are a little over 7,000 family child care providers in the city, and fewer than 2,000 are in a network.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: That leaves about 5,000 providers locked out of the contract seats.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: What are the specific steps to bring them in, and when do you plan?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: And why do the FCCs get paid less than a CBO for the same seat, also in the pay, and they have to pay a network fee?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: How do you expect to see them joining it as worth it?

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Thanks so much for your question, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: So New York City Public Schools contracts with networks, as you referenced.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: These are intermediary organizations, very often community-based organizations with deep roots in child care and in their community.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: We leverage networks as the vehicle to support home-based providers because administratively it is, as we all know, onerous to contract with the city and something that can be really challenging for a small child care provider.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: So the network takes on a lot of that administrative business work and then can provide support.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: to the provider when it comes to business enrollment and other administrative functions.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Our family child care networks are also equipped to provide coaching and support to family child care providers in languages that providers speak, which may be other than English.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: And so we believe that when they are operating at their best, our family child care networks are really

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: strong bridge to support providers participating in the city's initiatives.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: We also recognize that not all family child care providers have historically wanted to participate in networks.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: And so we've spent a lot of the past 10 months in conversation with providers and advocates who work with providers to understand what some of their challenges have been and working with them to identify

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: areas for strengthening our networks so that those can be more compelling opportunities for providers.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: We've really brought them the question of what would it take for you to be excited about joining a network and are working to incorporate the feedback we hear from them.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: I know you just referenced fees, and I know this came up at our last hearing.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Family child care networks should not be charging providers a fee for participating.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: And so if that's something you're hearing, we would love to follow up with your office and get more specifics because that is not part of the model.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: New York City Public Schools pays a flat rate to family child care networks.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: A portion of that rate is to cover their administrative costs, and the vast majority of that rate goes directly to the provider to cover services.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: If we plan on...

chapters.summary: Joseph asks why providers hesitate to join networks if the goal is universal child care. Liss says the city is expanding network capacity with 2K and engaging providers to address past hesitancies, myths, and real challenges.
chapters.title: Joseph asks why providers hesitate to join networks

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: If the goal is universal, you're leaving almost 5,000 providers out of that network.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: I know you said you're encouraging them to come in.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Do you know what the problem is as to why there's a hesitation to join your network?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Is that in conversation?

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Yeah, that's been a big part of the conversation is to say we are growing the capacity of our networks as we expand.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: So as we expand 2K, we are looking to bring family child care providers into the program in a significant way.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: We know that many families prefer home-based care for their toddlers, and that is a model we want to really lean on.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: So with the expansion of 2K, we are expanding network capacity and, again, really engaging providers to understand where there may have been past hesitancies.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: myths, misconceptions, and real challenges that we are working to address.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: I'm just going to thank you.

chapters.summary: Joseph asks about the nearly 30,000 families on voucher waitlists and how many of the promised 10,000 have been moved. Liss says about 3,000 invitations went out and families come off the list in order, with priority for those under 300% FPL, unhoused, or with a disabled child.
chapters.title: Joseph questions voucher waitlist and priority

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Nearly 30,000 families were on voucher wait lists this month.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Of the 10,000 children, the mayor promised to move off.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: How many have actually been moved?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Who got priority and how many families are still waiting once all the 10,000 are enrolled?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: I'm hearing from providers who are losing income while these seats remain empty.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: So as the administration announced earlier this month, we are beginning to take families off of the voucher wait list.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: We recognize that this wait list has been an incredible hardship for the families waiting for care and for the providers who are willing, ready.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: and able to serve those families.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Some portion of those 30,000 families may already be in other publicly funded care, but they absolutely have the right, if they would prefer a voucher, to remain on the wait list.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: We are inviting families to submit the paperwork to come off the wait list in tranches so that we can provide support.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: About 3,000 invitations went out to children on the wait list earlier this month, and we will continue to move families off the wait list.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: On a monthly basis until we maximize our funding.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: 10,000 is the number we shared at that announcement, but our hope is that we can continue to move even more families off the wait list.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: How do you prioritize the families you do move off the list?

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: So that is a process very tightly regulated by state and federal guidelines.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Families come off the wait list in the order they went on to the wait list.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: And families who come off the wait list must be in one of three priority groups, under 300% of the federal poverty line, unhoused, or the child has a disability.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: But we move through the wait list in order that families have been waiting.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Joseph asks whether the administration is walking women, women of color, and immigrant providers through MWBE certification and in their language of choice. Liss and Khan say SBS and NYC Public Schools have MWBE teams and encourage providers to seek certification.
chapters.title: Joseph asks about MWBE certification and language access

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Most of the child care workers are women, women of color, immigrants.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Is there, are you actively walking them through WMBE certifications?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: And if you are providing training for them, is it provided in their language of choice?

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: That's something you can speak to about broadly.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: I think we can certainly get back to you with more information about how our colleagues in the MWBE team talk about that, but if there's anything you want to add.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Yeah, the New York City Public Schools also has a MWBE team that works with their providers, but there's regular conversations between our team and their team.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: They do their own outreach, but we also have joined them and vice versa.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: And so there's a partnership between the teams that work on MWBE certification.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: We encourage any New Yorker, they don't have to go to public schools, they could also come to SBS and we'll help them with their MWB certification for sure.

chapters.summary: Joseph asks how the new RFP will close the pay gap for early childhood educators and whether current rates push small providers to keep wages low. Liss says wages are a major challenge, no new RFP has been released yet, and the city will work with council and labor on wages.
chapters.title: Joseph asks about pay parity and new RFP

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Labor is the biggest cost for these programs and turnover hurt children the most.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: How will the new RFP close the pay gap for early childhood educators?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: And is the current rate structure pushing small providers to keep wages low just to stay open?

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: So we know that wages and benefits are one of the biggest challenges that are facing child care providers and their workforce.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: And this is something we are committed to addressing over time.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: The city has not yet released a new RFP for early childhood services.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: That's something that will come.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: And we will be working with our partners in the council, our partners in labor to look at wages within that.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: And we are continuing to look at other pathways to support early childhood workers in the meantime.

chapters.summary: Chair Thomas-Henry asks whether the city tracks how many child care businesses are nonprofit versus for-profit. Liss says that data is not collected in licensing and that there is a healthy mix, with many for-profits operating on thin margins.
chapters.title: Chair Thomas-Henry asks about nonprofit vs for-profit data

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember Joseph.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: I have a couple of questions, and I'll turn it over to my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: I know you mentioned the number of child care businesses in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Do you have an account of how many of those businesses are nonprofit versus for-profit entities?

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: That is not a piece of data that the state or the city collect in licensing.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: We know there is a healthy mix of nonprofit and for-profit, and even among many of our for-profit businesses that they are very small businesses and, as was referenced, are operating on very thin margins.

chapters.summary: Thomas-Henry asks about liability insurance costs for child care providers. Liss says the office is very aware, hears it across the city, and is looking at ways to leverage city scale to address the crisis, noting few insurers remain in NYC.
chapters.title: Chair Thomas-Henry questions liability insurance

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Committee staff and subcommittee staff have heard that liability insurance continues to be an issue for child care small business owners, with 80% of child care owners nationwide reporting increased costs.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Is the Mayor's Office of Child Care aware of this issue, and are you offering any guidance to business owners in assessing affordable liability insurance?

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: We are very aware of this issue as we've gone across the city and met with child care providers of all sizes.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: This is something we hear as a really pressing concern.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: And as you noted, we know this is not just a New York City problem, but when I talk to child care leaders in other cities, it's something that folks are hearing broadly.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: We have been over the past couple months looking at ways the city can leverage

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: our scale and our power as city government to try and address this crisis because we know that it's really hurting our providers.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: So that's something we are actively working towards solutions on.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Have you talking to any providers in particular that would be interested in focusing on providing more affordable rates to child care businesses?

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: At this point, there are very few insurance companies operating in New York City that will insure child care providers.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: We want to make sure those who are in the business don't leave, but we also do need to look at alternatives to support providers.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: And again, this is something we see happening all across the country.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: where the number of insurers who are willing to back child care providers is dwindling.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Gotcha.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Next question.

chapters.summary: Thomas-Henry asks whether the Mayor's Office provides specific training for family child care home providers on operating as sole proprietors. Liss points to network coaching and a cooperative effort for home-based educators.
chapters.title: Chair Thomas-Henry asks about training for family child care sole proprietors

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: In family child care homes, business owners often wear multiple hats as both the early childhood educator and the business operations coordinator.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Is the mayor's office of child care providing any specific trainings for family child care home providers on how to operate a child care business as a sole proprietor?

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: So for family child care providers who are part of our family child care networks, they do receive access to coaching and support through their network.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: There are also many, many wonderful organizations operating here in the city who are incredibly skilled at the business of family child care who work with our family child care educators.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: And we are in close conversation with many of them about that.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: As I referenced the testimony, we are also working with a group of family child care educators who are interested in building a cooperative, which when stood up would be a vehicle to really support the participating members with all aspects of running their business.

chapters.summary: Thomas-Henry asks what services family child care networks offer to alleviate administrative burden. Liss says networks act as intermediaries with NYC Public Schools, handle contracting paperwork, and bear financial risk for providers.
chapters.title: Chair Thomas-Henry asks about family child care network services

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: What services do family child care networks offer to alleviate some of the business administration burden from these home providers?

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: So family child care networks serve essentially as the intermediary between New York City public schools and our family child care providers.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: They take on the burden of contracting.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: with the city, all the paperwork that is required in order to be a contractor with the

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: city, they bear the financial risk that comes with that as well.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: And so in that sense, are essentially providing greater stability for the providers than they might have if they were working directly with the city.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: At this time, right before I turn it over to Councilmember Gutierrez, I'd like to acknowledge that we've been joined by Councilmember Brooks Powers, co-chair.

chapters.summary: Councilmember Gutierrez asks again whether the city can collect nonprofit versus for-profit data. Liss says the city and state share licensing responsibility and she will follow up on what business information can be collected.
chapters.title: Gutierrez asks about nonprofit/for-profit data collection

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Thank you both for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I wanted to ask to the mayor's office of child care.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I know you referenced, I mean, in your testimony, roughly the amount of providers.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Do you have a sense of how many are nonprofit and how many are for-profit?

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: That is not information that the city or state actively collect.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Okay, sorry.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Do you, can you collect that information?

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: I would have to get back to you on whether that we can collect that.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: The city and state share the responsibility for licensing child care providers in the city.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Our family child care providers are licensed by the state and our center-based child care providers are licensed by the Department of Health.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: So we'd have to get back to you on what business information we can collect.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

chapters.summary: Gutierrez asks about private equity interest in child care and whether guardrails are needed for public funds. Liss says the office is watching it and points to co-ops and employee ownership as alternatives, but has not yet set guardrails.
chapters.title: Gutierrez raises private equity concerns and guardrails

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Is the mayor's office of child care, you all concerned about reports of increased interest from private equity in the child care industry?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I know we've heard from folks almost at every single hearing testify about that.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Yes, that is something that we are keeping an eye on.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Part of why we've been really excited about structures like this cooperative that we're discussing with child care providers is it's another way of providing business support and strength to providers

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: can often also be a model of that supports succession planning.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: We've been really excited by some of the more innovative business models we've seen popping up in the city.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: For example, Imagine Early Learning, which is the first fully employee-owned child care chain in the city.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: And we are very much keeping an eye on the growth of private equity into child care.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: We know that the strength of New York City's child care ecosystem.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: is that it is so deeply rooted in community, and we have providers who have been in their communities for decades and decades, and we want to make sure that that small business framework, that we continue to see providers with those community connections operating.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I think the concern is, right, it's just comparatively a private equity company that just has a more...

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: That you can see they have more funding for infrastructure.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: It's really difficult for a home-based provider two blocks away to compete.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Are you all thinking through this co-op, and I will ask more about this co-op, are you all thinking about guardrails around these private equity, still businesses, receiving public funds for childcare?

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: It's something we're certainly going to look into.

chapters.summary: Gutierrez asks about the status of the $3 million emergency microgrant program. Liss says the city is finalizing a contract with an administrator and plans to launch the provider-facing application by the end of the year.
chapters.title: Gutierrez asks about microgrant program status

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Okay, I wanted to ask about the microgrant program, which I think is great.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: You referenced it in your remarks.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Can you share the current status of this program?

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: So in August, we announced that we were launching this program by opening up a procurement for an administrator to actually run the program.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: So we are in the final stages of contracting with that administrator.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: We are also deep in the work of planning for what the microgrant program, all of the details of it.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: And we've had child care providers at the table driving that planning, you know, thinking about questions like what kinds of emergency expenses will be eligible and what.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: of grants, in what ways should providers be prioritized as they apply for the funding.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: And we plan to, with the administrator and with our advisory group of providers, launch the program later this year.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Okay, and when would it be, I know that you're in that procurement process, when would it be available for a provider potentially to apply?

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Our goal is to launch the provider-facing part of this program by the end of the year, and then we anticipate making grants on a rolling basis as providers experience emergencies and apply for those funds.

chapters.summary: Gutierrez asks how the city will ensure child care small businesses remain viable as universal child care expands. Liss says the priority is helping providers open, operate, and sustain, and notes 2K will be delivered entirely through community-based and home-based providers, not schools.
chapters.title: Gutierrez asks how small businesses remain viable in universal system

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: As the DOE early childhood system expands, not every family will immediately have access to public options.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And child care small businesses will continue to play a critical role in providing child care.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: How will you ensure child care small businesses remain viable as the universal system is set up so that the city doesn't lose our child care capacity?

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: It is absolutely a priority for us to make sure that child care providers, regardless of their relationship with the city, are able to continue opening, operating, and sustaining their businesses.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: We want to make it easier for them to open in the first place, which is why we've invested in things like the permitting portal to smooth the pathway to opening.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: We are also working to streamline the various processes and regulations where multiple agencies are involved so that providers are not kind of caught in the crosshairs between different agencies and conflicting guidance.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: office plays a role there.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: We want to make it easier for families to find child care providers through tools like nyc.gov slash child care, which is a map of every licensed child care program in the city and tools to help families find their way to those programs.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: And then as we continue to expand access to care, make sure we are prioritizing

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: work with our community-based child care providers and home-based providers, which is why with the expansion of 2K, we are working 100% with providers.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: There's no 2K in schools.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: This is a program entirely built in partnership with community-based child care providers and home-based providers.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

chapters.summary: Gutierrez asks if any child care businesses have closed due to lack of voucher access. Liss says it is a concern but she has no specific examples; Gutierrez says she will share a provider that closed in May.
chapters.title: Gutierrez asks about closures due to voucher lack

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I'm not sure if my colleague, Councilmember Joseph, I know she was talking about the vouchers, but are you aware of any child care business closing due to lack of families having access to vouchers?

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: It's a concern we've heard from providers.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: I don't have any specific examples of closures that have happened because of this.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Certainly, if there are any you're hearing about either in the district or elsewhere, I would love to talk about that.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: But we know that with the voucher wait list, obviously, it's placed a huge burden on families, but providers as well, particularly providers operating in lower income communities where families have historically relied on vouchers for care.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: So we know that reopening the wait list is something that will support families, certainly, but our providers as well.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: But so, okay, and you haven't heard, I'll make sure to give you the name of the provider that said they closed because they closed in May.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: because of the vouchers.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And the 10,000 or 10,000 plus, I think, is amazing, but I think it's not a system that families or even providers really know to depend on year after year, right?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: It's not something that's funded in the out years.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: The 10,000 is really just through the end of this fiscal year, correct?

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: No, the 10,000 families who receive vouchers as they come off the wait list, they will maintain a voucher for as long as they remain eligible, which is why we waited to begin taking families off the wait list until we had that certainty.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: We did not want to give families and providers access to care only to then have to take it away.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: So any family who receives a voucher, so long as they remain eligible, they will be able to maintain that voucher.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Okay, and then...

chapters.summary: Gutierrez asks whether funding for new families to come off the voucher waitlist is secure beyond this year. Liss says the 10,000 families who receive vouchers will keep them as long as eligible, but new families can still apply and funding is state-dependent.
chapters.title: Gutierrez asks about new families and state funding for vouchers

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: But new families who are adding, they're adding themselves to the wait list, correct?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: New families can continue to apply and add themselves to the wait list.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And that funding to support, to get those families off, newer families off the wait list, we're not sure about in the next year.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: So the Child Care Assistance Program, aka vouchers, is a state-funded program.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: And so we are able to take families off the wait list now as we leverage the funding we received from the governor earlier this year.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: And certainly that's something we'll continue to talk about with the state.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: But there's no, and I'm not trying to take away, I think the 10,000 is great.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I think it's worthy of the announcement.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: But I just want to be clear for New Yorkers who are hearing like, oh, there's 10,000 vouchers available now.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: It's 10,000 vouchers really working its way through this wait list.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: But if you are having a baby in the new year.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: and you're in need of this voucher, that doesn't mean that there is money for this voucher for you.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: I just want to be clear.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: The 10,000 or more vouchers that we are able to give out at this point will go to the families who have been on the wait list the longest.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: So we do expect there will still be families waiting for care.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And that's just leveraging with the state for their budget.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: We also want to make sure that for families who may be waiting for a voucher but may also be eligible for other forms of care, whether that's 2K, 3K, or pre-K,

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: or any of the city's Head Start or Early Head Start programs that families know about and are taking advantage of those care options, even if they elect to remain on the wait list for a voucher, they may be able to receive other care in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Yeah.

chapters.summary: Gutierrez asks about increasing voucher reimbursement rates. Liss explains the state sets market rates through a survey and is set to update rates in 2027.
chapters.title: Gutierrez asks about voucher reimbursement rate and market rate survey

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And is there any conversation with the state about increasing the reimbursement rate for these vouchers?

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: So the voucher reimbursement rate is set through by the state through a process called the market rate.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: And the state has recently issued their market rate survey to child care providers across the city, which is a chance for providers to inform the state about the cost of providing care.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: The state will use that data to then set the market rate and they are set to update their market rates in 2027.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I have a couple more and then we can, I know we've got a number of members.

chapters.summary: Gutierrez asks about the new Early Childhood Management System (ECMS) for contracted providers. Liss says DOE is actively developing it and she will defer to NYC Public Schools for an update.
chapters.title: Gutierrez asks about Early Childhood Management System

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Okay, in January, the administration testified that there was going to be a new payment and data management system rolled out by the DOE for contracted providers.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Is that system still on track to be launched by?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Now, the end of the year?

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: The DOE is actively working on the development of the system called the Early Childhood Management System, or ECMS, and would really defer to my colleagues at New York City Public Schools to give an update, which we're happy to provide to you and the subcommittee.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I think you answered this before.

chapters.summary: Gutierrez asks about contract rates, fixed costs like rent and insurance, and classroom ratios. Liss explains rates were negotiated in 2021, providers submit annual budgets, and ratios are standard for 2K, 3K, and pre-K.
chapters.title: Gutierrez asks about contract rates, fixed costs, and classroom ratios

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Besides what you, I think you referenced this in your testimony about the 2% increase, just referencing contracts, the 2% increase for CBOs, 5% for family child care networks in the process.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: When these rates were awarded, and of course I'm referencing the original bid in 2019 and 2021, when they were awarded, did it include an opportunity to negotiate a reimbursement for fixed costs such as rent or insurance?

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: So the contract, the rates that providers have in their contracts, which, as you said, were negotiated for many providers in 2021 when their contracts were first set, providers went through a rate negotiation process with New York City Public Schools.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: There was not one single rate providers.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: There is variation in between those rates and providers were able to demonstrate.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: for example, their rent costs as a way of informing their rate.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And is there, is that locked in or is there an opportunity for a provider to ask for higher reimbursement rates, such as increasing rent or labor costs?

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: There are, so providers'rates are set at the time of the contract and based on a budget that they develop.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Every year providers submit an updated budget to New York City Public Schools.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: If there are providers experiencing some significant shift in costs, you know, would encourage them to connect with their operations analysts at New York City Public Schools to look at their budget.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: But there is, and, you know, in moments where, for example, in 2024, when there was a new labor agreement between

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: DC 37 and the Daycare Council, providers with staff in the union received increased funding to support that collective bargaining agreement.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Does the current contract only reimburse programs for the minimum legal classroom ratio?

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Providers'budgets are set based on the classroom ratios that are dictated by the DOE, which is 18 children and two teachers for pre-K, 15

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: children and two teachers for 3K, and 12 children and two teachers for 2K.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: So it's only, but it's only, it's for, it's the amount.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: That is set across the board or that's set individual, like contract by contract?

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: That is the standard classroom group size and ratio for all 2K, 3K, and pre-K providers.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: There are some exceptions, for example, for integrated classrooms where there are children with disabilities learning alongside children without IEPs.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Gutierrez asks how the new RFP will address pay parity and low wages. Liss says increasing wages is a priority and the administration is eager to partner with the council.
chapters.title: Gutierrez asks about pay parity and new RFP

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I have one more question.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And I think you'll hear a lot about this from some of the folks that are testified, but obviously I want to once again raise dignified wages, pay parity.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And I know we're rather early, but I want to make sure that folks are encouraged to bring this to your attention.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: How will the new RFP seek to address pay parity and low wages for these early child care workers?

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Increasing wages and addressing some of the significant equity gaps we've seen is a priority for the administration.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: And we are looking at ways we can work to address that and eager to partner with council as we think about this in the coming year and years.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Gutierrez asks whether any new networks were established from the RFI. Liss says there were and she will get specific numbers from NYC Public Schools.
chapters.title: Gutierrez asks about networks RFI and new networks

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I have one more question just about networks, and I'll pick it back up after members.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: But can you just tell me from the RFI that was sent out earlier this year, were any new networks established as a result of the RFI?

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: There were, and I would have to work with my colleagues at New York City Public Schools to get back to you on the specific numbers.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Okay, great.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And now I'll turn it over to Council Member Felder for questions.

chapters.summary: Councilmember Simcha Felder raises chronic late payments to child care providers, saying he has heard from at least 10 providers unpaid for the previous year. Emmy Liss asks for the list and says new staff at NYC Public Schools are being hired to support invoicing and payment.
chapters.title: Felder raises chronic late payments to providers

utterances.speaker: Simcha Felder
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Simcha Felder
utterances.text: So first of all, I wanted to thank you and thank the administration for giving the attention to this area.

utterances.speaker: Simcha Felder
utterances.text: To my knowledge, this has been an area that I, you know, has certainly had my attention for

utterances.speaker: Simcha Felder
utterances.text: for quite some time and at least beginning with the de Blasio administration,

utterances.speaker: Simcha Felder
utterances.text: we didn't have, I never got a straight answer about the questions that are being raised this morning and the answers that have been given.

utterances.speaker: Simcha Felder
utterances.text: So despite the

utterances.speaker: Simcha Felder
utterances.text: despite the problems of not getting, being able to get it done, you know, immediately, I think that I appreciate at least that they're being addressed.

utterances.speaker: Simcha Felder
utterances.text: Having said that,

utterances.speaker: Simcha Felder
utterances.text: The issue of payment to the providers is something that I hear over and over and over.

utterances.speaker: Simcha Felder
utterances.text: And again, it's an issue that you inherited, you know, you need a SWAT team to really address because

utterances.speaker: Simcha Felder
