utterances.text: I think there are so many providers that are, you know, that just haven't been

utterances.speaker: Simcha Felder
utterances.text: paid for a long time.

utterances.speaker: Simcha Felder
utterances.text: So irrespective of what they should be getting paid, prospectively, if they haven't gotten paid and they have to pay the rent now and everything else,

utterances.speaker: Simcha Felder
utterances.text: You know, it is inherently, when you talk about closures or not closures, whatever it is, it's certainly making it impossible for them.

utterances.speaker: Simcha Felder
utterances.text: And that's something that I hear repeatedly.

utterances.speaker: Simcha Felder
utterances.text: And I'm not volunteering to give you a list because I can if you want one.

utterances.speaker: Simcha Felder
utterances.text: But there are, I would say.

utterances.speaker: Simcha Felder
utterances.text: You know, they're not in my district, but I myself, I would say, have heard from about conservatively at least 10

utterances.speaker: Simcha Felder
utterances.text: providers that haven't gotten paid for the previous year.

utterances.speaker: Simcha Felder
utterances.text: I'm not talking about...

utterances.speaker: Simcha Felder
utterances.text: 25 ending.

utterances.speaker: Simcha Felder
utterances.text: They still haven't gotten paid for the previous year, and it's not as though somebody has said, you're missing information.

utterances.speaker: Simcha Felder
utterances.text: In fact, one of them showed me the email with a compliment, you know, or some sort of saying, thank you very much for providing all the information needed.

utterances.speaker: Simcha Felder
utterances.text: And they're still waiting for the money.

utterances.speaker: Simcha Felder
utterances.text: So I'm not, again, the purpose is not to blame you, although I would love to, because that's a lot juicier than asking.

utterances.speaker: Simcha Felder
utterances.text: the question, but the fact is that you know, I mean,

utterances.speaker: Simcha Felder
utterances.text: and again, it's not something that started under this administration and that this administration, in effect, has to correct a problem that's been going on for at a minimum, I would say at a minimum, eight years.

utterances.speaker: Simcha Felder
utterances.text: I think more like 12 years or something like that.

utterances.speaker: Simcha Felder
utterances.text: So the question is,

utterances.speaker: Simcha Felder
utterances.text: I'm sure you're aware of this problem, and I just would like to know whether there's anything, you know, you had mentioned additional money or additional staff.

utterances.speaker: Simcha Felder
utterances.text: You talked about...

utterances.speaker: Simcha Felder
utterances.text: Additional staff, but in addressing a different problem.

utterances.speaker: Simcha Felder
utterances.text: It has additional staff been set aside or hired or whatever else to deal with providers getting paid.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: First, I would say do give us that list.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: If you have providers who have told you they've not been paid, please do share that with our office, and we will follow up immediately with the relevant agencies to make sure that that is looked into right away.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Some of the staff I referenced in testimony, the new staff lines that have been funded at New York City Public Schools, all of which are currently

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: in the hiring process right now or that already have been hired on.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Many of those staff directly support operations and work closely with providers on things like invoicing and payment.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: And really our goal in bolstering staff capacity is to make sure that we don't just accept that because payment has always been a slow process, it needs to continue to be one.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: And we want to make sure that folks are being compensated for the work they are doing.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: I know that there are also providers, including I know folks who are here to testify today, who have concerns about the payment timelines for vouchers, which is something our colleagues at the Administration for Children's Services are looking at really carefully and closely as well.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Council Member Brewer.

chapters.summary: Councilmember Gale Brewer asks about One Center Street's Little Apple child care program. Liss says it serves about 40 children of municipal employees, is free for employees, and is a model being watched for replication.
chapters.title: Brewer asks about One Center Street Little Apple

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Very articulate answers.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I have a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: First of all, what are you learning?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I have three kind of disparate questions.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: What are you learning from one center street, if anything?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: The second question is, with all of this great news, what kind of evaluation is being done to see if families are staying in New York?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Obviously, it's too early, but you've got to get started.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: The way evaluation works, as you know, you start from the beginning.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: If you start in the middle, it's not good evaluation.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So I want to know if that's happening.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And then third for SBS.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: You know, how many folks are you working with?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: How many child care businesses are existing in the private sector?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And there's one that I'm really interested in, which is the 24-hour for the folks at the airport and people who have lots of, you know, different kinds of jobs.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So that's just the beginning of questions.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: So first on One Center Street, the Little Apple, which started earlier this year, is now serving about 40 children, employees of municipal staff who work at One Center Street or elsewhere

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: as part of DCAS.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: The facility is gorgeous.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: I highly recommend stopping by.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: It's a great way to brighten your day if you've not been.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: And I think the feedback we're hearing from folks who have access to that is that it's been really wonderful to them.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So their pain or your pain?

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: It is completely free for the employees, and it is child care for kids under three.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And so the cost is something that would be replicable to others under three also, basically.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: So it's a model, you know, this is, it's the first, it's sort of the first of its kind, and it's something we're looking at closely to see the impact it has on city workers and whether it's a model that could be replicated ultimately.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: To your question, yeah.

chapters.summary: Brewer asks what evaluation is being done to see if families are staying in New York. Liss says families with children under six are twice as likely to leave, and the city is working with external researchers and EDC to monitor impacts.
chapters.title: Brewer asks about evaluation of family retention

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Yeah, the biggest, next one is, what about evaluation?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: So this is something very top of mind for us.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: I mean, as you referenced in terms of families leaving the city, part of the reason why child care has been such a focus for this administration is because we see that families with children under six are twice as likely to leave the city as other households.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I tell them to go to hell when they do, but yes.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: So we are working with a number of different outside research institutions who are all interested in studying the effects of our investments on child care in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So they're going to do it or they're getting funded to do it or where are we?

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: There are a couple of institutions that have outside funding to do this.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: We are also within the city working with the Economic Development Corporation and others to look at and monitor the effects of our investments.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: There are a few external research reports that we know are in work.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I prefer external.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Okay, we're doing both.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: And in the mayor's office of child care, we are really working to coordinate with all of the outside researchers who are studying this to make sure that all the questions.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: we have are being answered.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: And we'd be happy to share more about our nascent research agenda with you.

chapters.summary: Brewer asks about 24-hour child care. Liss says it is a big gap, few providers offer it, and family child care providers are more flexible, but more work is needed.
chapters.title: Brewer asks about 24-hour child care gap

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And then just 24 hour care.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Who's doing that?

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: So right now that that is a big gap.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: We know that there are families who because of their work schedules need that kind of care.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: We know that

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: There are not very many providers in the city who offer it.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Those who do tend to be our family child care providers because that's a model that is sort of more flexible, more able to meet those needs for families.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: It's something we need to spend more time and energy on, for sure.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Councilmember Santos-Oso.

chapters.summary: Councilmember Kayla Santosuosso asks whether the cooperative model could solve the insurance problem. Liss says the insurance crisis affects all providers and the co-op could provide shared buying power and services.
chapters.title: Santosuosso asks about cooperative model and insurance

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Thank you, both chairs.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: I want to turn to this, what I think is a really interesting idea about the cooperative, and ask you if there's any discussion on contemplating that model to solve the insurance problem.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: First, I would say I think we know the insurance problem impacts every provider in the city, regardless of their scale.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: So it's something we're looking at across the whole sector.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: I think we see the child care cooperative as potentially serving many functions, but one of them would be sort of shared buying power and shared services.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: How would that work?

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Would that work in conjunction with the centers, or do you see it solving different problems?

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Solving different problems.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: And I should say, I think cooperatives are a structure that we know are being looked at across sectors in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: So not just specific to child care, but it's a topic that's really on folks'minds in terms of how do we support small businesses.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: We are specifically working with a group of home-based providers who are looking at this model and whether it could apply particularly to support family child care.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Santosuosso asks how 2K seat distribution works. Liss says the city looks at the number of two-year-olds, historic enrollment, provider capacity, and existing Head Start programs to avoid cannibalizing services.
chapters.title: Santosuosso asks about 2K rollout seat distribution

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Turning to the 2K rollout, I think if I remember correctly, I don't know if it was at the press conference or if it was in one of these hearings, you were asked...

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Sort of the distribution of seats and how it would work.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: And I think your answer, I don't want to misrepresent you, but I think your answer was essentially that one of the factors is how many providers in each neighborhood or in each district actually sign up and are interested in being part of the program.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Am I representing that?

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: So that is a big part of that.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: So when looking at how many 2K slots should be essentially assigned to each of the districts that will have 2K, we look at how many two-year-olds there are.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: So, you know.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: So your district has a whole lot of two-year-olds versus some of our other districts that we are reaching next year just geographically are much smaller.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: And so we will look at anticipated demand.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss

utterances.text: We look at historic patterns of 3K and pre-K enrollment and other population factors to just sort of assess how many kids there are.

utterances.text: So right now we have our seat survey and our RFI both available to providers to assess interest in offering 2K services.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: We are also looking closely at what other care exists in communities for two-year-olds.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: For example, we have many early Head Start and Head Start providers across the city, and they provide incredible care to some of our lowest income families.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: And so we want to make sure that we're not cannibalizing services, but making sure that we're offering enough care in every community to serve two-year-olds who can use it.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Santosuosso asks how a home-based provider can find the right network and access materials in their native language. Liss says networks have multilingual staff and NYC Public Schools will host translated meet-and-greet sessions.
chapters.title: Santosuosso asks how home-based providers find networks and language access

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: I'm sorry, which of the networks the city contracts with if I wanted to express interest in being a part of this?

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Well, I'm happy to say, and we can share right after this hearing with all of you, we just posted a new sort of fact sheet for family child care providers.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: You know, you're interested in 2K, what next?

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Which does go through.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: through all of the different resources that providers have and the process by which they can identify networks that cover their geographic area.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Okay, great.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: And I know we already had the hearing on the dual language learners and the language capacity of some of these providers and of the program more broadly.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: If I were someone who ran a home-based, if I were a home-based provider and it was dual language and I wanted to be able to reach kinds of, you know,

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Many of our networks, our networks broadly have multilingual staff and based on the communities they operate in, the providers they work with, do have staff who speak many different languages.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: We will also, New York City Public Schools will be hosting sort of meet and greet sessions for networks and providers, which is something they did in the spring.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: And those sessions all will have translation support.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: That's great.

chapters.summary: Santosuosso asks what SBS can offer nascent home-based child care providers in immigrant and dual-language communities. Haris Khan says almost all SBS services are open to solopreneurs and the NYC Business Express team is being trained on child care licensing.
chapters.title: Santosuosso asks SBS services for nascent home-based providers

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: And for SBS, if there were very nascent early stage child care providers, particularly like home based providers, I'm thinking largely in immigrant communities or in dual language communities that wanted to get

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: in this process of getting themselves ready to become a part of this eventual program.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: What could they do?

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: What services could SBS provide for them?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Thank you, Council.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Members, so the vast majority, almost every single service that we offer, the general business services, they're all accessible to solopreneurs, home-based providers, to center-based providers, and all of them remain open.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: What we're really excited about in this calendar year under the mayor is the expansion of our NYC.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan

chapters.summary: Santosuosso asks about the SBS contract financing loan fund and whether it could help with late payments. Khan explains the fund offers 3% interest loans for city contractors; Liss adds child care providers are eligible for interest-free bridge loans through MOCS and the Fund for the City of New York.
chapters.title: Santosuosso asks about contract financing loan fund for late payments

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: and child care question, and this is half-baked, so bear with me.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: But, you know, the SBS program that is the sort of contractor fund where private equity loans in order to cover back payments for some city-based...

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Contracts.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Do you know what I'm talking about?

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: So we run a contract financing loan fund for city contractors who would want upfront capital to get started on the work that they would like to conduct.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: That's capped at a 3% interest rate, so it's very competitive compared to the market rate interest rates.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: And it's a revolving fund that we operate in conjunction with the Economic Development Corporation.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Is there a world where a model of something like that could help?

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Could work to solve some of the problems that we're facing with late payments and non-payments.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: In the child care sector.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: For our child care providers, and we saw this earlier this summer as folks were going through the contracting process,

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: our child care providers are all eligible for interest-free bridge loans that are offered through a partnership between the Mayor's Office of Contract Services and the Fund for the City of New York.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: That's a fund that's typically for nonprofits, but all of our child care providers are eligible for that.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: But they won't, and I know this because of personal experience dealing with some of this in my district, they won't be eligible for a bridge loan if they're being held up by permitting issues that originate with DOH.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: So if...

chapters.summary: Councilmember Frank Morano follows up on providers stuck in DOH permitting who cannot access bridge loans. Liss says the office triages these cases individually and asks for specific providers to follow up.
chapters.title: Morano follows up on permit issues blocking bridge loans

utterances.text: If the permit is still, and this is with not new providers, but that are going through some kind of renewal or there's a change in entity name, but if they're stuck in the DOH part of that,

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: And so we continue to kind of triage these on a one by one basis.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: And if there are specific providers in your district who are still sort of caught in this loop, please let us know and we can follow up on the particular cases.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilman Morano.

chapters.summary: Councilmember Virginia Maloney cites IBO data showing average ECE contract registration went from 83 days late in FY2021 to 247 days late in FY2024. She asks if the city reimburses providers for interest on loans; Liss says no, but interest-free bridge loans are available.
chapters.title: Maloney questions late contract registration and interest reimbursement

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Thank you, Chairs.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Thank you both for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Ms.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Liss, I was interested in your testimony about the $43 million investment to overhaul the city's early childhood education operations,

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: particularly the commitment to accelerate contract registration and prevent payment delays.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: A couple of my colleagues have alluded to this already, but according to the

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: independent budget office, the average early childhood education contract went from being registered 83 days after its start date in fiscal 2021

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: to 247 days after its start date in fiscal 2024.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: And again, I'm not blaming this administration for that.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: As my colleague said, you know, there's a lot of history here.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: But that's eight months.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Now, when the city doesn't pay a child care provider on time, that provider still has to pay the rent.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: They still have to pay employees.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: They still have to buy supplies.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: If a child care provider has to borrow money because the city hasn't paid what it owes them, does the city reimburse that provider for the interest on the loan?

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: So first I want to say that we've seen, as you said, not just in the most recent period, but over many, many years, decades, a sort of acceptance that it is okay to pay providers late.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: And that's something that we fundamentally want to change.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: We do not believe that represents the way the city should partner with child care providers, particularly given the time period you referenced where we saw contracting and payment, sort of that timeline protract.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: We saw a disinvestment in our early childhood infrastructure under the last administration, a nearly halving of the staff who support activities like contracting and payment.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: And that really drove a lot of the delays that we saw.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: And we are continuing to see some of the impact of that, though the investment you referenced that this administration is making is really targeted at addressing that, at making sure that we have the staff resourcing and support to pay providers in a timely basis.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: When a contractor, a child care provider has their contract registration delayed, they are eligible for interest-free bridge loans, and we really try and steer all contractors toward those loans because there is no,

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: then there's no additional cost that they have to bear to take those out.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: There is not, you know, if a provider takes out a loan on their own, that's something, you know, we're continuing to look into whether there are resources to support folks, but that's not typically part of the reimbursable expenses.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: So no.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Got it.

chapters.summary: Maloney asks how much of the $43 million investment is dedicated to on-time payments and what reduction in delays is expected. Liss says a meaningful number of new staff support payment and contracting, and the city will track registration and payment timelines.
chapters.title: Maloney asks about $43M investment and measurable payment delay reduction

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: So the city is effectively making a small business pay for the city's own inefficiency, right?

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: So of that $43 million that you're investing in reforms,

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: how much is specifically dedicated to making sure providers get paid on time, and what measurable reduction in payment delays are you expecting?

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: So I can get back to you on the exact breakdown of how many staff are assigned to payment and contracting, but that is a meaningful number of the new staff who are being invested in.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: There's also systems reforms.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Councilmember Gutierrez referenced the new sort of back-end data management system that the Department of Education is rolling out.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: And so there are sort of a number of investments specifically targeted, and we will look at things like contract registration timelines, payment timelines, you know, how long from the time of invoicing to the time of payment.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: We do see that process has improved meaningfully over the last number of years from the time a provider submits a fully complete invoice to the time it's paid.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: But certainly this year, you know, we saw that there's still much more we need to do on contracting.

chapters.summary: Maloney asks SBS whether the city calculated savings from the four child care reforms in the OPEN agenda. Khan lists the reforms and says SBS will work with agencies to determine if cost-savings analysis was done.
chapters.title: Maloney asks SBS about cost savings from child care reforms

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Mr.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Kahn, you know as a Staten Islander I'm not going to ask you any difficult questions.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: I appreciated your acknowledgement that the city's regulatory landscape can make life very difficult for child care business owners.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: You also mentioned the administration's open for small business reform agenda, which includes more.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: than 50 reforms and four specifically focused on child care.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Here's what I'd like to know.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Has the city calculated how much money those four child care reforms will actually save an individual child care provider?

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: So the reforms include a publishing of the plain language guide,

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: expanding the child care permitting portal, upgrading the background check request portal that's necessary for child care operators, as well as an office of child care, an ombudsperson office at the Department of Health.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: So some of them are structural investments in the city's infrastructure to support.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Some of them are resources for the business community, but have to work with the relevant agencies to determine if they've done any analysis on the cost savings.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: I look forward to seeing that because the reason I ask is because I think there's a real possibility we're spending taxpayer money subsidizing child care expenses that government bureaucracy helped create.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: In the first place.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: But may I ask one more quick question?

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Maloney raises the unintended consequence that publicly funded pre-K can raise infant care costs by removing older children who subsidize care. Liss says the administration is aware, is not placing 2K seats in public schools, and is working with providers to avoid destabilization.
chapters.title: Maloney asks about economic impact analysis on private providers

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: To Ms.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Liss, I want to raise something that doesn't get nearly enough attention.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Your testimony talks about the expansion of universal child care, including additional 2K opportunities.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: But the committee report points out an unintended consequence of these government-funded pre-K programs.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Older children are generally less expensive to care for, and the revenue from those

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Those children helps providers subsidize the more expensive infant and toddler care.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: When those older children move into publicly funded programs, the cost of infant care can actually go up.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: So before expanding government-funded child care,

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: into a neighborhood.

utterances.speaker: Virginia Maloney
utterances.text: Does the administration conduct any economic impact analysis on existing private child care businesses?

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: So this is an unintended consequence that we're very aware of, and I think certainly we saw play out in the city's expansion of pre-K and something that we are keeping very closely in mind as we design our continued expansion.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: So first, as we roll out 2K, we are not placing any 2K seats in public school buildings.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: We are only working with child care providers in communities to make sure that they are able to maintain the care that they provide to toddlers and that we are not creating any of that sort of.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Unintended effect of families moving out of community child care settings.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: We also saw there was an impact, an unintended impact here, particularly on our family child care providers with the rollout of pre-K,

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: because they were not at scale eligible to offer pre-K, which is tied to some state regulations, but certainly is a consequence we saw at the city level,

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: which is why we've been really intentionally focused on making sure that family child care providers have a seat at the table as we're rolling out.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: I think we want to be very careful in this set of expansions to balance the urgency that families have and the sort of desperate need families have for affordable or free care.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: But we need to make sure our providers remain sustainable.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Thanks very much.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: I'd like to acknowledge we've been joined by Councilmember Hanif.

chapters.summary: Chair Thomas-Henry asks whether the city has done a cost analysis for providing care from six weeks through 12th grade. Liss says the city is building toward a fully publicly funded system and has internal cost assessments but no specific figure yet.
chapters.title: Chair Thomas-Henry asks about cost analysis for six weeks through 12th grade

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: I want to kind of piggyback on my colleague's question as regards to starting universal child care, essentially, because as a parent, you can put your child in.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Daycare at six weeks old.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: So from six weeks old to two years old, literally the cost of daycare is roughly on the low end, $1,000 a month.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Roughly.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: On the low end.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: So have you guys looked at, ran a cost analysis from, kind of going back to your point, Council Member, so right now,

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: we know what three it costs to basically pay for a child from three years old, and in some instances, two years old, through 12th grade.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: You know what vouchers you are paying for now.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Has there been a cost analysis to determine what it would actually cost the city to take that six-week-old through 12th grade versus fighting the state every year for more money for vouchers and the like?

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Has that been done?

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: So part of why we are.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: What we are ultimately building toward is a fully publicly funded system that would care for all children or provide for the care of children starting as young as six weeks because, as you said, the costs are unbearable for families.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: And we believe that child care is and should be treated as a public good and funded that way from...

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: From the earliest ages that families may need to take advantage of care.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: We have some internal assessment of costs.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: That's something we're continuing to look at and to discuss with the state as we think about what the true pathway to universal child care would be.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: I don't have a specific figure to give you right now, but it's something that we have been closely looking at and kind of measuring.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: But it seems like literally my head is about to explode.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: From all the different nuances to how...

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Cost per child, this for that and that and this.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Yes, it's complicated.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: We have X number of, like, we're making a simple math problem, in my mind, way more complicated than it needs to be.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And it could be me.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: I could be wrong.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: But would really like to see how we could.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Simplify that because a lot of our parents are depending on that.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And as you can imagine, as my colleague reminded me, $1,000 per month per child is the low end.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Absolutely it is.

chapters.summary: Thomas-Henry asks which entities manage the bridge loan program and how providers access it. Liss says it is for providers contracting with NYC Public Schools, managed by the Fund for the City of New York, and applications go through the schools.
chapters.title: Chair Thomas-Henry asks about bridge loan program access

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: I wanted to ask a question as regard to the bridge loans.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Which entity or entities are you currently working with for that bridge loan program and how do child care providers get access to it?

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: So that is a

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: program available to providers who contract with the city.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: They, particularly providers who contract with New York City Public Schools, it was specifically available to cover the period before a provider's contract has been registered.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: So providers can work directly with New York City Public Schools to submit an application and that loan fund is managed by the fund for the City of New York.

chapters.summary: Thomas-Henry asks what is causing payment backlogs, noting providers waiting on city money. Liss says the city renewed over a thousand contracts this summer and historic disinvestment left insufficient staff, but the city tripled contract registration staff.
chapters.title: Chair Thomas-Henry asks about causes of payment backlogs

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: So not to belabor the point, but we've heard time and time again that the city is late and it's causing a lot of programs to close, cancel.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Literally got a phone call yesterday where some teachers aren't able to get paid because they're waiting on money from the city.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And some of these entities have been in business for 20, 30 plus years.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: What is causing these backlogs?

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: It seems like at this point in time, it should be like riding a bike.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: So, again, first I would say if you're getting a call like that from a provider, please feel free to flag that for our office right away and we can look into the particular situation.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: You know, we saw earlier in the summer that there was a delay in contract registration as the city was renewing over a thousand early childhood contracts.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: And so that's not a process that happens every year, but it is a process that we had to go through this year.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: And we saw the sort of legacy of this sort of historic disinvestment in our early childhood system.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: You know, we did not have the sufficient staff capacity to.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: And that was part of what drove the process.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: And we worked quickly.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: to address it by more than tripling the number of people who were working on contract registration, working to make sure providers were aware of bridge loans and other supports to ensure they had what they needed and to move through that process as quickly as we could.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Got it.

chapters.summary: Thomas-Henry asks SBS whether it offers funding solutions separate from bridge loans for payment backlogs. Khan points to the contract financing loan fund at 3% interest and notes the MOCS program is more generous.
chapters.title: Chair Thomas-Henry asks SBS about funding solutions for payment backlogs

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: For SBS, does SBS offer any type of funding solution separate and aside from the bridge loan program to child care providers when there is this backlog or absence of payment from the city?

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: So thank you, Chair Thomas Henry.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: So it's the we have the contract financing loan fund, but as Executive Director Liss mentioned that the mayor's fund and the mayor's office of contract services has an even more generous program and that it doesn't have an interest rate associated with it.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: The contract financing loan fund is one that has a 3% interest rate.

chapters.summary: Thomas-Henry asks about SBS hiring support and Workforce One placements for child care. Khan says SBS connects businesses to Workforce One centers and reports roughly 50 child care placements, with 18 centers across the city.
chapters.title: Chair Thomas-Henry asks SBS about hiring and Workforce One placements

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Also for SBS, through NYC My City Business website, it indicates that SBS can help a business with hiring a team and potential employers can request recruitment services.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Is this different from the Workforce One centers?

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: This is, so we have a...

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Our system is pretty integrated in that if we're helping a business owner and a business owner indicates recruitment assistance, we would then connect them with our Workforce One Center closest to them

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: and ensure that if we have more clarity on the types of roles they're hiring for, that we find them qualified candidates across the city.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Do you have an idea of how many child care positions are connected through Workforce One Centers?

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: can try to find that for you, Councilmember, but we have definitely served child care providers who have looked for support and hiring staff.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: If I don't have it on me, I'll get back to you with that number.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: I've also found that a lot of child care providers or child care entities often work with SBS, not SBS, SYEP students.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Do you guys track that as well in terms of placement with summer youth employment and where they're placed in child care facilities?

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: We can certainly follow up with our colleagues at DYCD and come back to you with data on that, but we do know that many youth are in child care programs through SYEP, and that's a great experience for both the youth and for the child care programs.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: We've mentioned and heard from a few people the expense of insurance.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Does SBS direct people that ask for selecting insurance for their child care business to any particular resource at all?

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: So, Chair, we don't direct businesses to particular for-profit businesses for any professional service that they're looking for, including insurance.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: But definitely something we've heard really loudly and clearly across the business community, especially the small business community, and something that Executive Director Liss mentioned is also prevalent in the child care industry where the cost of insurance is skyrocketing

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: in ways in which it's making it really difficult for folks to operate their businesses.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: I did have the number on job seekers placed every year.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: It's roughly 50 job seekers.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Child care, as we proceed with the universal child care expansion, we'd love to serve more providers who are looking for qualified candidates across the city.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: And we've got 18 centers.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: They're located all across the five boroughs and not too far away from neighborhoods.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: So please do reach out to us.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: If you know of any providers that are looking to staff up, we're definitely interested in helping them.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: So is that 50 people looking for jobs that have come through a Workforce One site this year?

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: No, 50 placements.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: 50 placements.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: I'm sure it's hundreds of New Yorkers, but it's 50 actual placements.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: And again, it's hard for us to require that the employers hire the individual, but what we do is job match, making sure that the business owner gets and the providers get qualified candidates that meet their needs.

chapters.summary: Thomas-Henry asks whether home-based providers can access commercial lease assistance. Khan says they are eligible if negotiating a commercial lease, but residential leases are not covered.
chapters.title: Chair Thomas-Henry asks about commercial lease assistance for home-based providers

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Would a home-based provider be eligible for the commercial lease assistance program?

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: A home-based provider looking to negotiate.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: For child care.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Yes, a home-based child care provider looking to negotiate a commercial lease.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: So if they're looking to move into a storefront for either to be a child care provider or for other types of business activities would definitely be eligible for commercial.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: And we've definitely helped child care providers in accessing commercial lease assistance in the past.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: I think the idea is if I have a one-family home and I dedicate half of that home

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: strictly for the child care facility, would that business be eligible for the lease program or does it have to be an actual physical storefront?

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: It would have to be a commercial lease, not a residential lease.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: The laws around residential leases, there's a lot of difference in the protections that the city and state have for residential leases as opposed to commercial leases.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Thomas-Henry asks about private equity pushing small child care providers out. Khan says SBS is exploring protections and interventions, including lease differences and cost drivers like insurance and rent.
chapters.title: Chair Thomas-Henry asks about private equity and small business pushout

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Now, private equity has become a growing presence in the child care ecosystem, specifically large-scale firms, and small business child care providers are more likely to exit the child care market.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: What, if anything, has the administration been doing to ensure that small businesses are not pushed out of the market, especially by private?

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: equity.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: I mean, I'll start and I'll then pass to our executive director, but on, from SBS's perspective, we do know that one of the pain points that businesses have, two major pain points that businesses have across

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: the city's most common industries, including the care economy, one would be financing, just having the resources to expand, grow capital, and then second would be just navigating the maze of regulations.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: And with this particular industry, we all have acknowledged at this hearing, there are more regulations than many other industries.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: And so to that end, our financing assistance team works to connect.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: any New Yorker entrepreneur to a set of affordable lending options.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: We mostly partner with CDFIs, community depository financial institutions that are not-for-profits looking, mission-aligned, trying to help small businesses succeed in the city.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: And we also have our NYC Business Express service team, the team that you met on October 2nd.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: It was their first day in office.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: The mayor swore them in.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Today was the day where they were, they've been trained on all of our major enforcement agencies and the rules and regulations associated.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Today was the day where they were getting trained on child care as well.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Should have brought them down.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Anything to add?

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: They're busy in training.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: No, we'll just reiterate that we, as we continue to expand publicly funded care in the city, our priority is making sure we are partnering with our community-based child care providers and small family child care providers who are, you know, the backbones of their communities.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: And so we are really focused on making sure that as we are expanding public funding opportunities, that we are working very closely with those providers.

chapters.summary: Thomas-Henry asks how the city tracks small provider openings and closures. Liss says licensing agencies track openings and closures but there is no centralized data; Khan says SBS tracks storefront activations but not home-based providers.
chapters.title: Chair Thomas-Henry asks about tracking provider openings and closures

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: How are you currently tracking the number of those small providers that are opening and closing each year?

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: So any child care provider who opens has to have a license or a permit for our family child care providers.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: That comes through the State Office of Children and Family Services.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: For our center-based child care providers, that comes through the Department of Health.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: And so both of those respective agencies are looking at openings and closures and our office partners with both of them.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: But is that data reported in some centralized way so that you can easily?

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: It's not data that I have in front of me today, but it's something that we are trying to look at more systematically and would be happy to share with the council as we look at that data.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And does SBS look at that data at all to track the number of small businesses that essentially are opening and closing in the child care?

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: So just across the board, across industries, we look at storefront activations, and we know that for home-based providers, we don't have the kind of data sets that other agencies would have.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: But on storefront activations and closures, that's something we're looking at very closely across the city.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Gotcha.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: I'll now turn it over to Councilmember Gutierrez.

chapters.summary: Gutierrez asks whether the Mayor's Office is systematically notified when center-based providers close. Liss says there is no systematic mechanism; the office hears from community members, elected officials, or providers directly.
chapters.title: Gutierrez asks about systematic notification of center closures

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And thank you, Chair, for raising the questions about closures.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I'm curious if in collecting the data you are also...

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I guess, I know it's not something that you have readily available, so totally fine, but just curious if when these providers have to close, whether, I'm talking about center-based primarily.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Because I think those are more visible.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Are you made aware?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Is the mayor's office made aware when they're closing?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Like through a systematic reason or like is it council members calling you frantically saying a center is closing?

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: There is no systematic mechanism, no.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: We do, you know, we hear from community members, we hear from elected officials, we hear from providers directly sometimes.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: But there is no sort of systematic way that we are notified if a provider closes.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: That's an independent business decision they're making.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: And so that's, and, you know, we may find out about it before, we may find out about it after.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And what about if they are contracted with the city?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And still closing.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: If they are contracted with the city, then that's something, you know, that they discuss directly with New York City public schools.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: And we are notified when that does come up.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Have you heard of any instances where center-based, contracted with the city, are closing?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: For any like late payments or any like, are you made aware of the reason why they're closing?

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Certainly, any time a provider comes forward and says that they have some operational concern and that it might lead them to close their doors,

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: New York City Public Schools, if they're a contracted provider, our office, in any case, we will often try to support and see if there's a way we can support that provider.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: We have not, that I'm aware of, had any program closures because of payment issues in the last couple months.

chapters.summary: Gutierrez asks about closures of contracted providers and whether the city knows the reasons. Liss says NYC Public Schools is notified for contracted providers and the office has not seen program closures due to payment issues in recent months.
chapters.title: Gutierrez asks about charter school closures and DOE notification

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And then my last question on closures.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I know that some of the 3K and pre-K sites in churches, for example, that takes a little bit of work through maybe the diocese.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: But in my district, a number of the Catholic schools are closed, and now there's charter schools in those sites, many of the Catholic schools that maybe had a 3K or pre-K program.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Are you...

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Are you made aware of when that closure happens?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Are you, is the administration made aware of that closure is happening and now there's a charter expansion because of it?

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: So if there is a program closure in a community, you know, we do look every year at what the capacity for pre-K and 3K and now 2K is in that community.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: With the seat survey that we have open right now to existing providers, we do ask about providers'interest to expand their capacity.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: And certainly if we see in a community that there's been some shift, you know, we will work to try and address if we suddenly have a large number of families who previously had access to care and no longer have access to care.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: You know, when an independent school chooses to close, there are many ways we might find out about that, whether that's because they tell us directly, again, because we hear about it from the community.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: But we are constantly trying to assess.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: You know, what the need is in a community.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: And if there is a contracted provider who closes, you know, certainly that's something New York City public schools would be able to factor into their planning.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Is there a certain amount of time that they're required to alert DOE if they're contracted with the city and then the parents?

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: I would have to get back to you on that.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Okay, great.

chapters.summary: Gutierrez asks about the child care permitting tool and whether it will be available for renewals. Liss says the tool is available for new center-based providers and renewal integration is under development.
chapters.title: Gutierrez asks about child care permitting tool renewals

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I just want a couple more questions on the child care provider, the permitting tool.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Will the tool be available for permit renewals in the near future?

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Yes, that's something we're actively working on.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And I'm sorry, I missed.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Is this tool...

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Is this available now or?

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: So this is the tool we demoed for the subcommittee back in April or May.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: It is available for any center-based provider, prospective center-based provider looking to newly open in the city.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: And we are working to add renewals for center-based providers into this program as well.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And do you have a sense of when you'll be able to integrate the renewals?

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: That development work is underway right now.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: We can provide the subcommittee with an update.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Next, I just had questions on...

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Some of the operational costs.

chapters.summary: Gutierrez asks about food costs and whether the administration will supplement CACFP funding. Liss says future contract rates will consider food costs and notes the $40 million rate increase as a first step.
chapters.title: Gutierrez asks about food costs and CACFP supplement

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: In their recent report on the true costs of ECE programming by UNH, they highlighted food costs, especially for standard day-year programs, as an issue because federal funding through CACFP only covers income-eligible children.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Has the admin considered supplementing this funding?

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: You know, as we look at future contract rates, we will look at things like the cost of food and how to address that in contract costs.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: We do know that providers are facing rising costs, which is why the administration invested $40 million this year to make that 2% increase in center-based contract rates.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: We know that's just a first step and there's more that providers need.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Gutierrez asks about increasing funding for coaching and training. Liss says future procurements and rate setting will look at all cost categories, and NYC Public Schools provides instructional coordinators, social workers, and inclusion specialists.
chapters.title: Gutierrez asks about coaching and training funding

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And in the same report, UNH highlighted the fact that providers could use more coaching and training for support.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Is that something that the admin has also considered increasing funding for?

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: So the administration, you know, again, we, as we look ahead to future procurements and to future rate setting, we will look at all of the different cost categories that providers face.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: We do also, New York City Public Schools provides significant coaching and support to programs.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: So we have a team of instructional coordinators as well as a team of staff.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: social workers, and inclusion specialists who all go out and directly support programs.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: And that's capacity we've continued to build up and grow to make sure that we are able to support all programs as the city's contracted capacity grows.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Gutierrez asks about the home-based provider co-op and whether non-network providers can thrive in 2K. Liss says the co-op is exploratory, the city does not want home-based providers to close, and she will visit Bushwick to meet with providers.
chapters.title: Gutierrez asks about home-based provider co-op and non-network pathways

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And then my last questions for you, Emmy, were just related to the co-op.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: You mentioned, and I know this is in the beginning stages, so is it, you said it's primarily home-based providers that are kind of coming up, coming together for it?

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Yes, there's a group of home-based providers who are coming together to do some sort of exploratory work and planning for a co-op.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Okay, and is this, these are, I'm assuming, these are home-based providers and not in a network or a mixture?

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: I believe it's a mixture.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: As you know, and I always raise the deep concern that I have for continuing to expand this program without...

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: These independent business owners at the table.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I'm curious if there's any more, is there anything more that you can tell us right now?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: If I am someone who's looking to start my own home-based childcare center space in my home, but I don't wanna be a part of a network today, August 2026, do I have,

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Do I have the support of the administration to still be able to thrive in a 2K 0 to 2 space?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: If I'm in District 32, for example, in Bushwick, that is getting 2K seats, which is a great thing.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: But if I'm not already in the system, how can I?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: How can I still be successful?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: How can I still be a successful business owner?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: How can I do that in this climate?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Like, what are some of the things that you are all thinking about, I know, early on to kind of integrate these people so these businesses don't have to close down, so these primarily women don't have to kind of figure out another career option?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I'm very concerned for them.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: I mean, we absolutely do not want our home-based child care providers to close.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: We know how important these providers are to the families they serve.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: We know what their businesses mean to their communities, and we want to make sure that they can continue to thrive.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: I'm excited to come to Bushwick to sit with some home-based providers with you, hopefully in the coming weeks.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: And we've been, since January, meeting very regularly with home-based providers across the city and continuing to talk with folks about the concerns they have, about what they need in order to be successful,

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: and to really take their feedback to how we can continue to improve the structures and systems we have, including the networks, to make it a more appealing prospect, to make it something that can really deliver for our providers.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: There are many providers who are serving families with vouchers, are serving families who pay privately, and also working with the DOE through a network.

utterances.speaker: Emmy Liss
utterances.text: And we want to continue to support all of those pathways for our providers.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Thank you, Emmy.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: A few more questions for SBX.

chapters.summary: Thomas-Henry asks about implementation of the Red Tape Relief Act (Intro 955) for coordinated inspections. Khan says the law takes effect in February 2027 and SBS is scoping requirements and demand.
chapters.title: Chair Thomas-Henry asks about Red Tape Relief Act implementation

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: The council recently passed the Red Tape Relief Act, Introduction 955, earlier this year.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: That law is intended to coordinate inspections for specific businesses, especially businesses within the child care industry.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Has there been any updates on implementation of this bill from the mayor's office?

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And if so, are there any specifics that you can give in regards to how the program will operate?

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: So the bill goes into effect in February of 2027, so we have four months until the effective date.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: We're currently scoping what would need to be done at SBS to fulfill the requirements and understanding the demand that we would see from child care providers, and so that's where we're currently at.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: But we're excited for the expansion of our BEST team, and today was the day that they were trained on child care as well, so looking forward to this work.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Give me one second.

chapters.summary: Thomas-Henry asks how many child care providers have used the commercial lease assistance program. Khan says at least 35 businesses have used the full legal services program since the pandemic, though attorney-client privilege limits details.
chapters.title: Chair Thomas-Henry asks about commercial lease assistance usage

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Have any child care providers been assisted through the commercial lease program, assistance program?

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: If so, how many and what issues were addressed specifically?

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: So our commercial lease assistance program, since it's a legal service, there is some

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: attorney-client privilege is applied to some of those interactions.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: So we may not know fully the extent of and the depth of the service-related issues that the child care providers raised, but we do know that child care providers have used that service, as have other small businesses.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Since the pandemic, it's at least 35 businesses that we know that have used the commercial lease assistance program.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: You said 35?

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: It's 35 that have used the full legal services program focused on commercial lease.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: We know that with the expansion that this administration is leading, we're looking forward to serve a lot more.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And that's 35 since when?

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Since the beginning of the program, which was around the pandemic.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Thomas-Henry asks whether SBS conducts targeted outreach to child care providers and what materials are shared. Khan says outreach is broad and not industry-specific, but SBS helps with licensing, permitting, and financing.
chapters.title: Chair Thomas-Henry asks about SBS outreach and data tracking

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And does SBS conduct any outreach specifically targeting child care providers?

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And what type of materials are shared with those providers during that outreach?

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: So we conduct ground outreach that even, as you're aware, October 1st, September 1st, when we did the business owner bill of rights outreach or the street vendor outreach that we've done in your district.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: We go out, we're serving all types of small businesses, including street vendors, storefront businesses, entrepreneurs, New Yorkers that show up to our tables and our

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: mobile outreach unit asking to get connected with entrepreneurship services, even if they don't currently own a business.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: So our outreach work is one where we're focused on ensuring that we're reaching neighborhoods that are

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: far away from our business solution centers and even around our business solution centers.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: It's not one where we're targeting specific industries, but one where we're trying to make sure the broad variety of New York small businesses and entrepreneurs are able to take advantage of these services.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Because most of our services are not limited to a particular industry.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Any New Yorker could benefit from, that's an entrepreneur, could benefit from financing assistance, understanding what the affordable lending options are in the market, could benefit from some licensing and permitting support.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: We're proud to help child care providers and other businesses understand the DOB, FDNY rules and regulations and permitting that they would have to navigate.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
