utterances.text: And that's the type of support we provide across the...

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: ecosystem.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And does SBS currently track the number of, say, restaurants versus child care, apparel, and all the other industries, the different services that they provide to each individual?

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Yes, it really varies depending on the service that we're providing.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: So we'll have disaggregated data for the

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: deeper services such as the commercial lease assistance program.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: We won't have that for some levels of our business consultation or networking events or workshops that we organize where we just want

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: to make sure that they take advantage of the educational materials and wouldn't want to create another wall where they'd have to go through an intake process before they get served.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: At this time, I want to ask Shauna Castillo to join the panel.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: I have a couple of questions as it relates to NYCHA and SBS and the like.

chapters.summary: Thomas-Henry asks how many businesses SBS or BEST worked with in Business Pathways or owned by NYCHA residents. Khan says SBS tracks business location, not residency, and served about 4,000 businesses in NYCHA zip codes last fiscal year.
chapters.title: Chair Thomas-Henry asks about SBS/NYCHA Business Pathways coordination

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: How many businesses has SBS or BEST worked with that are part of the Business Pathways program or are businesses owned by NYCHA residents?

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: And I'll get you the number of businesses that operate within the zip codes that have the most NYCHA developments where we do services.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: We have an incredibly strong working relationship and coordination with NYCHA's REIS team that Vice President Castillo runs.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: And our work is one where, through our best team and through all of our services, we're not necessarily tracking the residency of the New Yorker that we're serving, but we're tracking the business location.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: And so it's hard to know if the New Yorker that we're serving is one who lives in public housing, but we are tracking the addresses of the businesses that we're helping.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: And so where they're located is something that we do see, and it's around 4,000 businesses just this last fiscal year around public.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: In what capacity has SBS worked with NYCHA, and does SBS provide any services to the Business Pathways program?

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: So the program was started in 2014, and at that time it was grant-funded.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: SBS, EDC, and NYCHA worked together in delivering, administering, developing the program.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Around the time of the pandemic, the program, or...

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Sorry, when grant funding expired, that's when NACHA took over administration of the program, but we still coordinate as needed on the program, just as we do with all other sister agencies when they run programs related to business activation.

chapters.summary: Thomas-Henry asks how many NYCHA residents are involved in Business Pathways. Shana Castillo says since 2014 there have been 365 food graduates and since 2015, 149 child care graduates; this year one child care cohort will enroll 25 residents.
chapters.title: Chair Thomas-Henry asks about NYCHA Business Pathways graduates and current cohort

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: How many NITRA residents are involved in the Business Pathways program, and how many NITRA entrepreneurs were assisted through this program this year?

utterances.speaker: Shana Castillo
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair, and thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: Shana Castillo
utterances.text: Since 2014, we have had 365 graduates from our Food Business Pathways program, and since 2015, 149 graduates from Child Care Business Pathways.

utterances.speaker: Shana Castillo
utterances.text: This year we are administering one cohort of child care business pathways that will enroll 25 residents.

chapters.summary: Thomas-Henry asks whether Business Pathways offers other sectors. Castillo says not currently, but NYCHA hosts monthly orientations and refers residents to partners like SBS for other business interests.
chapters.title: Chair Thomas-Henry asks about other Business Pathways sectors and advertising

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Are there any other programs aside from the food-based business and the child care provided in through the program, the Business Pathways program?

utterances.speaker: Shana Castillo
utterances.text: Not currently provided through Business Pathways, but we are a resource for NITRA residents that are interested in entrepreneurship in other sectors.

utterances.speaker: Shana Castillo
utterances.text: And so, for example, we'll host monthly resident business development orientations.

utterances.speaker: Shana Castillo
utterances.text: We'll invite speakers and partners out that can engage with residents.

utterances.speaker: Shana Castillo
utterances.text: And we do have a network of referral partners, including SBS, that we can refer residents to if they have a business interest or need that it's outside of the two sectors that we currently serve under the Business Pathways program.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: How are all these programs advertised?

utterances.speaker: Shana Castillo
utterances.text: They're advertised digitally and traditional flyering.

utterances.speaker: Shana Castillo
utterances.text: And so we do have a team that will flyer in NYCHA communities.

utterances.speaker: Shana Castillo
utterances.text: We'll also table at NYCHA-based events.

utterances.speaker: Shana Castillo
utterances.text: Also external events when invited.

utterances.speaker: Shana Castillo
utterances.text: We have a biweekly newsletter that goes out to all NYCHA residents that have provided NYCHA with an email address.

utterances.speaker: Shana Castillo
utterances.text: And we'll also lean on our communications team for social media content.

utterances.speaker: Shana Castillo
utterances.text: Lastly, I'll say that we know that word of mouth and really hearing real testimonies makes a world of difference.

utterances.speaker: Shana Castillo
utterances.text: And so we leverage our digital newspaper, our NITRA journal, to make sure that we're working closely with the comms team and producing

utterances.speaker: Shana Castillo
utterances.text: a variety of success stories every month for NITRA residents that also then link to how they can learn more about the program that was featured.

chapters.summary: Thomas-Henry asks how the programs are advertised and what percentage of NYCHA developments are reached. Castillo says advertising includes flyers, events, a biweekly newsletter, social media, and the NYCHA journal, and they hit every development.
chapters.title: Chair Thomas-Henry asks about advertising reach and data by development

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And of all the night your housing throughout the city of New York, what percentage of those actually participate or do you advertise to?

utterances.speaker: Shana Castillo
utterances.text: We're hitting every night to development.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And how many business owners do you have data in terms of by development, how many participants there are?

utterances.speaker: Shana Castillo
utterances.text: We'll maintain data on how many participants have engaged in Reese's programming, specifically in business pathways.

utterances.speaker: Shana Castillo
utterances.text: And so that will not only include who graduated, but also which businesses obtained their license in the case of child care or registered their business in the case of food.

utterances.speaker: Shana Castillo
utterances.text: And then NYCHA overall would obtain data through annual recertifications on the number of

utterances.speaker: Shana Castillo
utterances.text: residents that are reporting self-business income.

chapters.summary: Thomas-Henry asks about MWBE certification assistance. Castillo says NYCHA connects residents to Section 3 business certification and partners with SBS on MWBE promotion and hands-on sessions.
chapters.title: Chair Thomas-Henry asks about MWBE and Section 3 certification

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: As part of your toolkit, is there any assistance with MWBE certification for these businesses?

utterances.speaker: Shana Castillo
utterances.text: We certainly connect residents to our procurement team for registration as a Section 3 business concern, which is not an MWBE certification,

utterances.speaker: Shana Castillo
utterances.text: but it is a certification that NYCHA leverages.

utterances.speaker: Shana Castillo
utterances.text: And then additionally, we will work with SBS on promotion around MWBE certification.

utterances.speaker: Shana Castillo
utterances.text: In the past, we've actually hosted sessions in our computer lab where residents can get hands-on support in the certification process.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with Section 3.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: What is that?

utterances.speaker: Shana Castillo
utterances.text: Oh, it is just a designation for low-income workers and NITRA residents.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Thomas-Henry asks about large infrastructure projects near NYCHA developments and resident access to jobs. Castillo says she is not familiar with specific projects but NYCHA works with companies to share employment opportunities.
chapters.title: Chair Thomas-Henry asks about infrastructure projects and resident employment

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: So I'm going to give you, for instance, currently there's a few large infrastructure programs in my backyard, and there are...

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Two major Niger facilities, the Bland and the Latimer, within a one-mile radius.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Do you know offhand if any of these residents have access, be it to any of the employment opportunities or on-site work that's being done with the soccer stadium?

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And or will it's point?

utterances.speaker: Shana Castillo
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with those specific projects, but I can say that generally we are open to working with any company that wants to make sure that local residents are aware of their employment opportunities.

utterances.speaker: Shana Castillo
utterances.text: And we do so on a regular basis.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: In that, for instance, with so much infrastructure and development happening across the city, is there any current or future plans for training to prepare NITRA residents for those opportunities, be it as entrepreneurs or the workforce?

utterances.speaker: Shana Castillo
utterances.text: In our REIS department, we do offer a variety of job training initiatives through partners.

utterances.speaker: Shana Castillo
utterances.text: And so a popular and consistent one that we've offered is a construction track through the NYCHA Resident Training Academy.

utterances.speaker: Shana Castillo
utterances.text: And this is a pre-apprenticeship track.

utterances.speaker: Shana Castillo
utterances.text: And so it can connect residents to.

utterances.speaker: Shana Castillo
utterances.text: Union careers in the construction industry.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Awesome.

chapters.summary: Thomas-Henry asks how many staff work on Business Pathways and the program's fiscal cost. Castillo says REES has 55 staff, with one assistant director, two project managers, and two temps on business development; baseline cost is $100,000 per cohort.
chapters.title: Chair Thomas-Henry asks about staffing and fiscal costs of Business Pathways

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And how many staffers are in the business pathway programs?

utterances.speaker: Shana Castillo
utterances.text: The Department of REIS has 55 staff members total, and so staff members are cross-trained so that they can be supportive across functional units.

utterances.speaker: Shana Castillo
utterances.text: Specifically within our financial capability and business development team, we have one assistant director, two project managers, and two temp staff currently.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: the fiscal course of the program.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And for the last three fiscal years,

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: For the last three fiscal years, sorry.

utterances.speaker: Shana Castillo
utterances.text: So the baseline costs for child care and food business pathways is $100,000 for each cohort.

utterances.speaker: Shana Castillo
utterances.text: And so that cost, the fiscal year cost would depend on how many cohorts we operated in a particular year.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And how long is each cohort?

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And that 100K, is it a specific number of people that it can participate?

utterances.speaker: Shana Castillo
utterances.text: So our Child Care Business Pathways program is generally operating for 15 weeks, food generally operating for 10 weeks, and so these meet

utterances.speaker: Shana Castillo
utterances.text: about two times a week in the evening for two to three hours each session.

utterances.speaker: Shana Castillo
utterances.text: And I'm sorry, could you repeat the second part of that question?

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Number of applicants who can participate for that $100,000.

utterances.speaker: Shana Castillo
utterances.text: So we generally enroll 25 a cohort in child and 30 in food.

chapters.summary: Thomas-Henry asks about training format, application, and selection. Castillo says training is hybrid, 15 weeks for child care, and applicants attend an info session, apply, and are scored by a committee.
chapters.title: Chair Thomas-Henry asks about training format, application, and selection

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And where is the actual training based?

utterances.speaker: Shana Castillo
utterances.text: Well, since COVID, we actually switched to a hybrid method.

utterances.speaker: Shana Castillo
utterances.text: So we're doing a lot of virtual training and then place-based training depending on the topic and the needs.

utterances.speaker: Shana Castillo
utterances.text: So, for example, in child care, there is CPR and first aid that's done.

utterances.speaker: Shana Castillo
utterances.text: For food, we'll go and...

utterances.speaker: Shana Castillo
utterances.text: Take the aspiring entrepreneurs on a tour of a commercial kitchen, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: Shana Castillo
utterances.text: So it could operate in a variety of places, dependent on

utterances.speaker: Shana Castillo
utterances.text: the topic, but it's quite accessible now as a hybrid model.

utterances.speaker: Shana Castillo
utterances.text: And we've really seen since COVID that it's been quite helpful for residents to keep to that.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: How does someone apply and then how are those applicants selected?

utterances.speaker: Shana Castillo
utterances.text: So we'll identify in our promotional material how residents can learn more.

utterances.speaker: Shana Castillo
utterances.text: This typically starts with an information session, and so they may call our REIS hotline number, or they may also utilize a NYCHA self-service platform.

utterances.speaker: Shana Castillo
utterances.text: So authorized residents do have access to a self-service platform where they can RSVP for an information session event.

utterances.speaker: Shana Castillo
utterances.text: At the events, we'll provide an overview of the program, take questions.

utterances.speaker: Shana Castillo
utterances.text: From there, there is an application process, and we have a score grid that will follow, and then a small committee that includes our staff plus partner staff that can

utterances.speaker: Shana Castillo
utterances.text: evaluate applications.

chapters.summary: Thomas-Henry asks about Intro 445 and NYCHA's position on expanding Business Pathways. Castillo says NYCHA appreciates SBS partnership and would like more in-depth conversations with the council about the program.
chapters.title: Chair Thomas-Henry asks about Intro 445 expansion and NYCHA position

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Now, an introduction 445 from Councilmember Stevens would require the Department of Small Business Services to expand the Business Pathways program.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Is SBS at all involved in the Business Pathways program currently?

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And should they be, if not, should they be involved?

utterances.speaker: Shana Castillo
utterances.text: We are very appreciative of SBS's partnership.

utterances.speaker: Shana Castillo
utterances.text: They've been a long-standing partner to NYCHA, both on the workforce side and on the business development side, and we absolutely leverage them as a referral partner.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And what is NYCHA's position on this bill?

utterances.speaker: Shana Castillo
utterances.text: We appreciate the council's interest in the business pathways program.

utterances.speaker: Shana Castillo
utterances.text: We are very...

utterances.speaker: Shana Castillo
utterances.text: Encouraged at what we see in continuing the program and definitely have successes of resident graduates from there.

utterances.speaker: Shana Castillo
utterances.text: We'd love to set up more in-depth conversations with the council members in order to really discuss the program as it currently operates.

chapters.summary: Thomas-Henry asks about resident feedback and program adjustments. Castillo says feedback led to introducing the state licensing application during classroom time rather than after graduation, especially for digital access needs.
chapters.title: Chair Thomas-Henry asks about resident feedback and program adjustments

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: What has the residents'feedback been thus far of the current Business Pathways program?

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And do you solicit feedback as part of the program?

utterances.speaker: Shana Castillo
utterances.text: We have taken feedback to make adjustments to the program.

utterances.speaker: Shana Castillo
utterances.text: So an example of that will be the point in time in which we introduce the state application for licensing for child care businesses when we first started the series.

utterances.speaker: Shana Castillo
utterances.text: We did that as like a postgraduate service.

utterances.speaker: Shana Castillo
utterances.text: And the feedback was that it is very overwhelming and it's really good to make use of classroom time in order to start that process and get hands-on support, particularly as the application has now become digital.

utterances.speaker: Shana Castillo
utterances.text: We do have residents that have a digital literacy or digital access need.

utterances.speaker: Shana Castillo
utterances.text: So that's an example of how we'll incorporate feedback into the program.

chapters.summary: Thomas-Henry asks where a home-based provider can get financing help. Castillo says the next child care cohort will offer microgrants for furnishing, and NYCHA refers providers to SBS and other partners for financial assistance.
chapters.title: Chair Thomas-Henry asks about financing help and microgrants

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And if a home-based provider needs help with financing, where would you direct them?

utterances.speaker: Shana Castillo
utterances.text: So we do see that providers need help with financing generally.

utterances.speaker: Shana Castillo
utterances.text: Specifically for child care, our next cohort in November will actually offer micro grants for

utterances.speaker: Shana Castillo
utterances.text: a select number of graduates from the program that can help with things such as like furnishing that they need that are specific to the child care business that they're intending to operate.

utterances.speaker: Shana Castillo
utterances.text: So depending on the need, then we'll make a referral to SBS or to other partners that can then provide further financial assistance and guidance.

chapters.summary: Thomas-Henry asks whether NYCHA has done a cost analysis for expanding Business Pathways under Intro 445. Castillo says new sectors would require a new cost analysis, and resident interest remains highest in food and child care.
chapters.title: Chair Thomas-Henry asks about cost analysis for expansion

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And going back to Introduction 445, have you done a cost analysis or began to think about what it would look, the cost would be associated with expanding the program?

utterances.speaker: Shana Castillo
utterances.text: Certainly, we know that depending on what we are considering for expansion, so for example, new sectors would require a new cost analysis that we have not yet done.

utterances.speaker: Shana Castillo
utterances.text: We're first led by resident interest and surveying residents.

utterances.speaker: Shana Castillo
utterances.text: They're consistently interested.

utterances.speaker: Shana Castillo
utterances.text: They maintain interested in starting a business and identifying needs around business coaching and capital, as you previously stated, as needs that they have.

utterances.speaker: Shana Castillo
utterances.text: to be successful, but they also consistently identify food and child care as being a primary interest of theirs, and that's why we've really stuck to offering this program series.

utterances.speaker: Shana Castillo
utterances.text: As stated previously, we know that a baseline cost for this particular industry of food or child care would be

utterances.speaker: Shana Castillo
utterances.text: And then, of course, that cost could potentially rise if we're discussing the expansion of microgrants in the program, like I previously mentioned.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Two final questions for me, and then turn it over to my colleague.

chapters.summary: Thomas-Henry asks how many child care businesses opened through Business Pathways are still operating. Castillo says 149 have graduated since 2015 and 57 opened businesses.
chapters.title: Chair Thomas-Henry asks how many child care businesses still operating

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: How many of the businesses that you guys helped open for child care specifically are still operating?

utterances.speaker: Shana Castillo
utterances.text: So as stated previously, we've had 149 graduates of child care since 2015, and 57 of those graduates have moved on to opening their business.

chapters.summary: Thomas-Henry asks whether NYCHA tracks how many business owners remain in NYCHA housing. Castillo says NYCHA periodically surveys owners and refers those who move out to partners like SBS.
chapters.title: Chair Thomas-Henry asks about tracking NYCHA residency of business owners

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And have you began tracking or seeing of these business owners how many continue to reside in NYCHA versus any who may go on?

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Moved out?

utterances.speaker: Shana Castillo
utterances.text: So periodically we will survey business owners to reach out, see if they need continued support, confirm if they're still operating.

utterances.speaker: Shana Castillo
utterances.text: You are right, one of the reasons that we will see for a business to drop off from operating might be that they moved out of NYCHA.

utterances.speaker: Shana Castillo
utterances.text: In that case, if they're still interested in business services, we would direct them to partners such as SBS.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Got it.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: At this time, I'll turn it over to Councilmember Gutierrez.

chapters.summary: Gutierrez asks Castillo to explain the Business Pathways industries and training focus. Castillo says the program covers food and child care, helping residents start or formalize businesses, including home-based child care.
chapters.title: Gutierrez asks Castillo about Business Pathways industries and training focus

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair, and thank you, Ms.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Castillo.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I may ask a couple of questions that sound really elementary because I'm not familiar with the Business Pathways program.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Can you just tell me what are the...

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: What are the industries?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: you're able to train people for in this program?

utterances.speaker: Shana Castillo
utterances.text: Our most common industries are food and child care, and that aligns with resident interests.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And what's the food industry?

utterances.speaker: Shana Castillo
utterances.text: So food...

utterances.speaker: Shana Castillo
utterances.text: Usually looks like catering, but not necessarily.

utterances.speaker: Shana Castillo
utterances.text: And so we do have business operators that might sell their products in retail market as opposed to catering.

utterances.speaker: Shana Castillo
utterances.text: So that's why we call it food broadly.

utterances.speaker: Shana Castillo
utterances.text: But it is a program that it is not teaching you culinary skills, but it's a business development program for residents that are looking to start or formalize their food business.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And for the child care portion, that is helping people start their business of child care in their homes.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Elsewhere or particularly to help them set up for opening up in their homes in Nigeria?

utterances.speaker: Shana Castillo
utterances.text: Opening up in their homes and or formalizing their business.

utterances.speaker: Shana Castillo
utterances.text: So it is recognizing that there could be some informal businesses that are happening.

utterances.speaker: Shana Castillo
utterances.text: And this is also making sure across the board that, you know, residents begin to understand.

utterances.speaker: Shana Castillo
utterances.text: Like babysitting or nanny service?

utterances.speaker: Shana Castillo
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: Shana Castillo
utterances.text: If you occasionally babysit, there's a way to really build on that and really formalize a business.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: But it is for specifically in the other respect, it's for them to be able to like set up their home.

utterances.speaker: Shana Castillo
utterances.text: In their apartment, correct.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Gutierrez asks SBS about private equity contracting and whether the city needs guidelines for working with private equity versus local small businesses. Khan says he defers on contracting to MOCS but SBS is exploring protections and interventions.
chapters.title: Gutierrez asks SBS about private equity contracting and protections

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Okay, I'm going to come back to you.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: But I just wanted to ask SBS.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I raised this to the mayor's office of child care before about private equity, and we do hear a lot.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: We hear them almost at every hearing.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And some of those firms are contracted with the city, right?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Some of them, they're part of the universal model.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: But does SBS, in your effort to support small businesses, do you feel that there are any...

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Do you think that we should be creating more guidelines for the way that the city works with contracts with private equity versus actual small, you know, local community businesses?

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: So on contracting, I would have to defer to the Mayor's Office of Contract Services and Chief Procurement Officer Kim Yu, but on the topic of private equity and the impact it's having across

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: the small business industries, it's something we're hearing, we're seeing, and we're working really hard to figure out ways to avoid and come up with ways that the city could use its power, either purchasing power or

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: other interventions, programmatic interventions or protections that the city should consider to support small businesses.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: And so there's work underway in the next couple of months.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: You'll hear more on how we could do better to protect small businesses.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And, okay, do you have any examples of, like, specific protections that you're thinking about?

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: It's a whole host of things that we're currently exploring.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: And one thing we're also looking at that brief.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: came up earlier in this conversation was on leases.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: There's differences in residential leases and commercial leases, and why is that and why have we accepted the norms on one set of leases on types of protections landlords are liable for and the types of protections landlords are liable for in commercial leases.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: So that's just one area of interest.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: There's other areas that we're looking at.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Certainly the cost of insurance has come up significantly for so many small businesses.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: The cost of commercial rent has come up across the city.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: And so we're looking at how can the city government not just look at the things city government can do to reduce the cost drivers for them, which are things that you've heard, looking at fines, looking at fees, looking at process, but also look at things that are beyond the direct control of city government.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: But is there a role the city can play?

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: Our viewpoint here is we should be as expansive as possible in delivering relief for small businesses, and that's what the commissioner and the administration is intending to do.

utterances.text: Is there, with regards to child care, private equity, I've been meeting with them, speaking with them, a lot of them,

chapters.summary: Gutierrez asks what a New Yorker should do to open a child care business. Khan says there is no wrong door: SBS helps with storefront openings, works with the Health Department, and notes mandatory orientation and viability checks before leasing.

utterances.text: And then I know that you mentioned earlier there's kind of your limitations, I guess, with supporting just a child care business.

utterances.text: But is there something on if I guess what is a direction for a New Yorker who wants to open up a child care business?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: They just open up their laptop and are they using my city?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Are they going the SBS route?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Kind of what is like the next step if someone's just like blindly saying like, I want to open up a child care business in New York City?

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: I think there's no wrong door.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan
utterances.text: If folks approach SBS, we will help them, especially with storefront business openings.

utterances.text: That's something where we've got resources, services, technical assistance, and we work very closely with the Bureau at the Health Department that does the licensing.

utterances.text: So before you even think of getting your lease or you get your licenses, you first learn a whole set of regulations.

utterances.speaker: Haris Khan

utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.text: Castillo.

utterances.text: Again, this is like brand new information to me.

utterances.speaker: Shana Castillo
utterances.text: And then we currently do partner with SBS and absolutely can continue to strengthen our partnership with them, particularly as they take on new pieces of this work in the current administration.

chapters.summary: Elena Knishnikolson, educational director at a DOE-contracted preschool, details her budget, rent, teacher salaries, and pay disparity with DOE centers. She calls for pay parity and asks the city to stop treating early childhood educators as free child care.
chapters.title: Elena Knishnikolson testifies on preschool budget and pay parity

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elena Knishnikolson
utterances.text: My name is Elena Knishnikolson, and I'm an educational director in a preschool that is contracted with DOE.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elena Knishnikolson
utterances.text: We have one pre-K and two 3K classrooms, 46 kids altogether, three teachers plus four assistant teachers, one floater.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elena Knishnikolson
utterances.text: I wish it was a full-time assistant teacher, director of operation, and at last me.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elena Knishnikolson
utterances.text: My budget is $900.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elena Knishnikolson
utterances.text: 14,000 a year for 10 months.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elena Knishnikolson
utterances.text: The biggest expenses is my rent, which is $30,000 a month.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elena Knishnikolson
utterances.text: Out of those $38,000 is our share of property taxes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elena Knishnikolson
utterances.text: Our yearly rent is $3,060,000 and DOE covers $2,046 of it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elena Knishnikolson
utterances.text: My teachers are making $72,063 and $59,000, which is $1,094,000 a year.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elena Knishnikolson
utterances.text: If they were working in DOE Center, not CBO, their pay would be $1,000.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elena Knishnikolson
utterances.text: would be without experience, $80,000 and $71,000.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elena Knishnikolson
utterances.text: So the difference in one year is huge.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elena Knishnikolson
utterances.text: In 10, it is a fortune, a down payment for an apartment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elena Knishnikolson
utterances.text: Assistants are being paid $30,000 for full-time and a floater gets $20,000.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elena Knishnikolson
utterances.text: $1,000, $40,000 right there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elena Knishnikolson
utterances.text: Director of operation gets $30,000 and my salary is $75,000 a year.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elena Knishnikolson
utterances.text: Altogether, it comes to $442,000 a year.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elena Knishnikolson
utterances.text: If you add those two numbers, it's $688,000 a year.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elena Knishnikolson
utterances.text: And while that number sounds like a budget of a small town, when you divide those numbers by the hours people put weekly, you are getting chump change.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elena Knishnikolson
utterances.text: I do pay into my staff's medical insurance, 401k, disability insurance, and unemployment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elena Knishnikolson
utterances.text: And then there's food bills, electricity, fire alarm, internet, phone, maintenance, liability insurance, janitorial supplies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elena Knishnikolson
utterances.text: The biggest issue in early childhood education are qualified staff, and this is where my budget fails me.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elena Knishnikolson
utterances.text: In one of the council meetings in the summer, I bumped into my city college professor, Gail Buffalo, and I said that the issues we talked about 13 years ago are unfortunately the same.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elena Knishnikolson
utterances.text: The biggest one is pay parity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elena Knishnikolson
utterances.text: DOE can do better for all of our staff and stop calling early childhood education educators free child care.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elena Knishnikolson
utterances.text: Please start paying all my staff the same as, say, our DOE pre-K center neighbors with three classrooms, Little Brooklyn.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elena Knishnikolson
utterances.text: And while many of you are calling for more hours in early childhood education,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Elena Knishnikolson
utterances.text: early childhood education, I have to remind you all, we too have families and our kids need us too.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Those were a lot of numbers.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Can you provide the written testimony as well?

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Okay, there you go.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Thank you for coming and staying.

chapters.summary: Abigail Leonard of Children's Aid testifies on the liability insurance crisis, noting core liability premiums doubled from 2022 to 2026. She urges support for a resolution on state legislation and for the Office of Insurance Affordability to examine child care and nonprofit human services.
chapters.title: Abigail Leonard testifies on liability insurance crisis

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Abigail Leonard
utterances.text: Good afternoon, chairs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Abigail Leonard
utterances.text: My name is Abigail Leonard, and I am Policy and Communications Analyst at Children's Aid.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Abigail Leonard
utterances.text: Children's Aid provides early childhood, foster care, behavioral health, youth development, and other services to children and families across New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Abigail Leonard
utterances.text: Across this work, we've seen how the liability insurance crisis threatens the business model of child-serving organizations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Abigail Leonard
utterances.text: The crisis is particularly severe for voluntary foster care agencies, which provide state and locally mandated services.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Abigail Leonard
utterances.text: But more broadly, we're concerned that rising insurance costs will weaken provider infrastructure needed to responsibly scale child care services across New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Abigail Leonard
utterances.text: At Children's Aid.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Abigail Leonard
utterances.text: Our core liability premiums doubled from 2022 to 2026.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Abigail Leonard
utterances.text: Between 2023 and 2025 alone, our primary general, professional, and sexual abuse and molestation coverage rose from approximately $594,000 to $1.2 million.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Abigail Leonard
utterances.text: Our umbrella and excess coverage nearly tripled from $206,000 to almost $630,000.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Abigail Leonard
utterances.text: This has direct implications for the business of child care.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Abigail Leonard
utterances.text: Government-contracted child care providers may be required to maintain specific insurance coverage, but they cannot simply raise their

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Abigail Leonard
utterances.text: prices when premiums increase.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Abigail Leonard
utterances.text: Their revenue is largely determined by government contracts and reimbursement rates that may not reflect current insurance costs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Abigail Leonard
utterances.text: Providers are left to absorb the difference within already constrained program budgets.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Abigail Leonard
utterances.text: These costs affect real business decisions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Abigail Leonard
utterances.text: When more funding must go toward insurance, providers have less flexibility to invest in wages, retain educators, maintain facilities, open classrooms, or expand it to communities with unmet need.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Abigail Leonard
utterances.text: If a required coverage becomes unaffordable or unavailable, it can also determine whether an organization can compete for a government contract or continue operating the contracted program at all.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Abigail Leonard
utterances.text: We urge the Council to support Council Members Gail Brewer and Althea Stevens'forthcoming resolution calling for the passage of important state legislation to address this problem, and to ensure the new Office of Insurance Affordability examines the challenges facing child care and

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Abigail Leonard
utterances.text: nonprofit human services providers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Abigail Leonard
utterances.text: The city's child care system cannot expand if the organizations expected to operate it cannot afford the basic cost of doing business.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Abigail Leonard
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Megan Shantz, owner of Supermoon Art Space in Ridgewood, says her center is under-enrolled for the first time as families cannot afford care. She worries 2K funding may only cover minimum staffing and asks how to connect with voucher families.
chapters.title: Megan Shantz testifies on under-enrollment and 2K concerns

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Megan Shantz
utterances.text: My name is Megan Shantz.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Megan Shantz
utterances.text: I'm the owner and director of Supermoon Art Space, which is a small center-based daycare in Ridgewood in Queens.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Megan Shantz
utterances.text: We're in our ninth year of operating, and we've cultivated an excellent reputation in our community.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Megan Shantz
utterances.text: However, this year, for the first time, we are under-enrolled because middle and lower-income families we aim to serve can no longer afford to pay for care.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Megan Shantz
utterances.text: We're faced with the possibility of taking out loans, possibly laying off staff to cover costs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Megan Shantz
utterances.text: And while we're submitting our proposal to become a 2K program next year, simply sustaining the business between now and a possible contract in July is proving to be a huge challenge.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Megan Shantz
utterances.text: And should we receive a 2K contract, we're concerned about the issue that Council Member Gutierrez raised earlier about funding only covering the minimum number of staff required by Article 47.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Megan Shantz
utterances.text: We have cultivated a high-quality program with little to no staff turnover or burnout by employing a large team of teachers and administrators more than the minimum requirement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Megan Shantz
utterances.text: So the switch to 2K may not accommodate our ability to sustain that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Megan Shantz
utterances.text: We currently have space for families with child care vouchers and are so glad that more vouchers have recently been made available.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Megan Shantz
utterances.text: But we're not aware of a system that helps us connect with the families who've received vouchers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Megan Shantz
utterances.text: Calls to ACS and other local support networks have led to dead ends.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Megan Shantz
utterances.text: We would love to learn from the people in this room how a center like ours can locate voucher families in need of

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Megan Shantz
utterances.text: Additionally, as a form of expanding and growing our business, we've piloted a series of much-needed after-school programs for 3K and pre-K students in public schools.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Megan Shantz
utterances.text: They're fee-based programs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Megan Shantz
utterances.text: We also offer sliding scale rates and accept vouchers, but we would love to offer them for free.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Megan Shantz
utterances.text: However, we've learned that DYCD does not currently fund programs for children under six.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Megan Shantz
utterances.text: We sincerely hope that the city is considering modifying this restriction as part of a plan to provide universal child care.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Megan Shantz
utterances.text: I'd like to thank Councilmember Gutierrez and Councilmember Thomas Henry and this subcommittee for creating the opportunity to share these thoughts with you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Megan Shantz
utterances.text: And thanks for everyone in the room.

chapters.summary: Chair Thomas-Henry asks the panel about insurance contract increases and whether they have been denied higher amounts. Abigail Leonard explains liability insurance is paid across the organization and subject to administrative caps.
chapters.title: Chair Thomas-Henry asks panel about insurance contract increases

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: We just have a couple of quick questions for this panel.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: In regards to insurance, in your contract, have you increased the amount you're asking for and been denied?

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Or within the contract, you're not only allowed to bill for a certain amount?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Abigail Leonard
utterances.text: So liability insurance is very interesting because we pay for it across our entire organization.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Abigail Leonard
utterances.text: So we can't break it up between child care related liability insurance costs, foster care related liability insurance costs and whatnot.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Abigail Leonard
utterances.text: So we reference our insurance numbers in various ICR rates that we are able to have adjustments for.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Abigail Leonard
utterances.text: We're also a Head Start provider, and there is a 15% administrative cap for our ability to include contract or administrative costs, including insurance in that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Abigail Leonard
utterances.text: And our various contracts are our district.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Abigail Leonard
utterances.text: spread on how much we're able to claim and then how much we're able to adjust also.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Another complicated math problem.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And then I was going to say, in terms of vouchers and connecting to providers, Emmy and her team is still here right behind you.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Please connect.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: And Councilmember Gutierrez had some questions.

chapters.summary: Gutierrez asks Megan Shantz about under-enrollment and whether she is in a network. Shantz says the economy is the main cause, families are switching to family-based care or nannies, and she is not in a network but is applying for 2K.
chapters.title: Gutierrez asks Megan Shantz about under-enrollment and networks

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Just for you, thank you so much for testifying once again and for leaving your business to be with us all day.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: You said that for the first time you're under-enrolled.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And can you talk to me a little bit more?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: What is the reason?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Why do you think?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Megan Shantz
utterances.text: I think it's honestly the economy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Megan Shantz
utterances.text: I've had families that lost jobs in the past couple of months and had to either leave completely or reduce their days.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Megan Shantz
utterances.text: Because we're center-based and our costs are pretty high, we do charge slightly more than family-owned or family-based centers or family child care centers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Megan Shantz
utterances.text: So we have had families switch to family-based.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Megan Shantz
utterances.text: We have some families who had their first child with us, and now with their second child,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Megan Shantz
utterances.text: They have a nanny, and the nanny helps them at night with laundry and food.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Megan Shantz
utterances.text: And so they've just chosen to stay with the nanny rather than send their second child to us.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Megan Shantz
utterances.text: So we have a community of people, but I think my understanding is it's mostly the economy, that people are losing work and that the rates that we're charging, which we're trying to keep as affordable as we can, are just all...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Megan Shantz
utterances.text: all of a sudden out of reach for them.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And you're District 24, correct?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: So it's one of the sites.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And you are not in a network?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Megan Shantz
utterances.text: We're not.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Megan Shantz
utterances.text: We've reached out to networks, but we were not, for whatever reason, I don't know if we're not eligible.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Megan Shantz
utterances.text: It wasn't really part of our plan from the beginning because operating independently was working for us.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Megan Shantz
utterances.text: We don't really turn a profit, but we've been able to sustain.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Megan Shantz
utterances.text: And like I said,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Megan Shantz
utterances.text: Part of the reason that makes it difficult to sustain is because we have a really big team.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Megan Shantz
utterances.text: And that makes it easier for everyone that's on our team to feel comfortable and nurtured and supported, but it just makes it really expensive to operate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Megan Shantz
utterances.text: And we've had to raise rates just to accommodate that.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And do you have a universal 3K or pre-K program?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Megan Shantz
utterances.text: We don't.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Megan Shantz
utterances.text: We didn't apply for 3K when it came through.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Megan Shantz
utterances.text: We just have been serving two-year-olds primarily, but now we are applying for 2K.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Megan Shantz
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Well, let's continue to stay in touch.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I just know from my constituents who are alum just rave about your site.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And this is a lot of the work that we try to highlight at these hearings is someone who's operating, yes, an independent business, but really this like...

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Foundation for our families.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: It's the reason why I'm sure the majority of your families are from the neighborhood, but you've got families that are traveling far and wide, and these are like quality programs that we want to make sure not only just stay open, but can thrive in this universal child care program.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: So thank you.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Thank you both so much.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Megan Shantz
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Panel is excused.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: The next panel, Drew Weber, Ingrid Matias, Shelby Lohr, and Shanita Bowen.

chapters.summary: Ingrid Matias Chungata, Executive Director of Nuestros Niños, testifies on 53 years of service and delayed reimbursements that left staff unpaid for weeks. She calls for predictable contracts, timely payments, and equitable per-child funding.
chapters.title: Ingrid Matias Chungata testifies on Nuestros Niños and delayed reimbursement

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ingrid Matias Chungata
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ingrid Matias Chungata
utterances.text: Good afternoon and thank you for the opportunity to testify today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ingrid Matias Chungata
utterances.text: My name is Ingrid Matias Chungata and I'm the Executive Director of Nuestros Niños, proudly serving Williamsburg and Queens for the last 53 years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ingrid Matias Chungata
utterances.text: I want to begin by acknowledging the city's recent commitment to improving early childhood.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ingrid Matias Chungata
utterances.text: Particularly the investment in contracting payment systems and expanding services to our families.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ingrid Matias Chungata
utterances.text: These are encouraging steps, but as we move forward toward universal child care, we must strengthen the foundation of the systems, the community-based organizations, and family child care educators who make it possible.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ingrid Matias Chungata
utterances.text: And nuestros niños, we know firsthand the challenges of delayed reimbursement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ingrid Matias Chungata
utterances.text: Our staff and our providers were without pay for a couple of weeks this summer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ingrid Matias Chungata
utterances.text: And certainly the uncertainty of contracts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ingrid Matias Chungata
utterances.text: Yet our responsibility to our children, our families, and our employees never stopped.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ingrid Matias Chungata
utterances.text: We need predictable contracts, timely payments, transparent systems, and equitable per-child funding that reflects the true cost of quality education, regardless of where the child lives

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ingrid Matias Chungata
utterances.text: and who serves them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ingrid Matias Chungata
utterances.text: And we cannot overlook our family child care providers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ingrid Matias Chungata
utterances.text: These are small business owners who are hoping their homes, invested their resources, and dedicated to servicing their community.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ingrid Matias Chungata
utterances.text: They deserve equitable compensation, business stability, and a meaningful voice in decision that affects their livelihood.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ingrid Matias Chungata
utterances.text: Community-based organizations are equally essential.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ingrid Matias Chungata
utterances.text: We are not simply contracted providers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ingrid Matias Chungata
utterances.text: We are part of the fabric of our neighborhoods.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ingrid Matias Chungata
utterances.text: We know our families, their cultures, their history, their language, and their needs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ingrid Matias Chungata
utterances.text: As the city reimagines early childhood education, I urge us to build a system grounded in partnership, shared accountability, and a respect for every child care provider.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ingrid Matias Chungata
utterances.text: Because universal child care is not just about expanding access, it's about ensuring that institutions and educators, families, and trusted generations are supported, valued, and positioned to strive.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ingrid Matias Chungata
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Shanita Bowen of ECE on the Move testifies on payment reversals and late reimbursements for family child care educators. She urges increased rates, modernized payment systems, notice before reversals, and reasonable repayment plans.
chapters.title: Shanita Bowen testifies on payment reversals and late reimbursements

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanita Bowen
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chairs Thomas Henry and Gutierrez.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanita Bowen
utterances.text: My name is Shanita Bowen, Chief Operating Officer for ECE on the Move.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanita Bowen
utterances.text: We represent family child care educators in residential settings across New York City and the families that they serve.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanita Bowen
utterances.text: We are educators and small business owners.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanita Bowen
utterances.text: We pay taxes, employ staff, and keep parents working.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanita Bowen
utterances.text: Our businesses are struggling to survive.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanita Bowen
utterances.text: Families can't afford the true cost of care, and reimbursement rates don't cover our operating costs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanita Bowen
utterances.text: And yet, we face two payment problems.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanita Bowen
utterances.text: First, unexplainable payment reversals.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanita Bowen
utterances.text: One educator's reimbursement was reversed without adequate explanation or the educator's input.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanita Bowen
utterances.text: Even after the city's system error was corrected, it took an entire month for her payment to be restored.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanita Bowen
utterances.text: This should never happen.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanita Bowen
utterances.text: Educators deserve notice and an opportunity to resolve errors before the reversal occurs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanita Bowen
utterances.text: Even when a reversal is justified due to the educator's error, reasonable repayment plans must be available so that the business can continue to operate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanita Bowen
utterances.text: Second, late reimbursements.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanita Bowen
utterances.text: Our outdated attendance and payment system need modernization and better management.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanita Bowen
utterances.text: Payroll and expenses don't wait.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanita Bowen
utterances.text: pay late with when we receive our pay late with I'm sorry when we when we pay our bills late we get penalized but when our reimbursements arrive late who compensates us for

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanita Bowen
utterances.text: the hardship how can we expect essential small businesses to stay open when the system they dependent

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanita Bowen
utterances.text: on are so unpredictable.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanita Bowen
utterances.text: We urge the council, ACS, and the state to increase reimbursement rates, expand child care assistance, modernize the payment system, prevent unexplained

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanita Bowen
utterances.text: and explain reversals, offer reasonable repayment plans for educator errors, and end late reimbursements through greater accountability.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanita Bowen
utterances.text: True universal child care means more than access.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanita Bowen
utterances.text: It requires systems that work together to support families and the educators who serve them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanita Bowen
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Drew Weber of the Consortium for Worker Education describes CWE's child care scholarship program, which pays higher rates and full enrollment rather than attendance. He calls for better pay for providers and stronger connections between programs across city agencies.
chapters.title: Drew Weber testifies on CWE and child care scholarship

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Drew Weber
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair Gutierrez, Chair Thomas Henry, and members of the committee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Drew Weber
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to testify.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Drew Weber
utterances.text: My name is Drew Weber, and I work at the Consortium for Worker Education, or CWE.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Drew Weber
utterances.text: As the workforce development arm of the New York City Central Labor Council, we train home-based and union child care workers and run two programs connecting working New Yorkers to subsidized child care.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Drew Weber
utterances.text: In that work, we have seen firsthand how the current system underserves both providers and parents.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Drew Weber
utterances.text: We need a system that pays reliably and fairly and is made easier to navigate for everyone involved.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Drew Weber
utterances.text: Earlier this month, alongside the UFT, CLC, ILR, and Providers Organized for Power, we convened union leaders and child care providers to discuss how to build a universal...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Drew Weber
utterances.text: child care system that works for all workers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Drew Weber
utterances.text: Ideas included many of what was discussed today, including a shared service cooperative, pay ladder to guaranteed fair wages, care for workers working non-traditional hours, and child care benefits negotiated directly into union contracts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Drew Weber
utterances.text: What was clear is that we cannot leave behind the workers and providers who have been at the front lines of this work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Drew Weber
utterances.text: We have seen firsthand how better and more reliable pay can make the difference for providers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Drew Weber
utterances.text: CWE's state-funded child care scholarship program supports middle-income, episodic, and undocumented families who don't qualify for the child care assistance program.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Drew Weber
utterances.text: Notably, it pays out higher rates than what is allowed under CCAP, and it pays for a child's full enrollment rather than based on attendance, so a provider is indicted when a child is out sick.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Drew Weber
utterances.text: For a small business running on thin margins, that means steadier income and greater financial stability.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Drew Weber
utterances.text: We have also seen how hard it is for parents and providers to navigate assistance programs split across three city agencies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Drew Weber
utterances.text: Along with better pay for providers, we urge the city to build stronger connective tissue between these programs, either internally or through partnerships with nonprofits, so parents, providers, and unions know their options.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Drew Weber
utterances.text: We look forward to continuing our work with advocates, unions, and the council to build a universal child care system that works for all workers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Drew Weber
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Shelby Lohr of the Daycare Council of New York testifies on late and unpredictable contract payments. She cites a 2023 survey where 64% of providers were unpaid for the prior month and 26% took personal loans to bridge gaps.
chapters.title: Shelby Lohr testifies on Daycare Council survey and late payments

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shelby Lohr
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair Gutierrez, Chair Thomas Henry, and members of the Subcommittee on Early Childhood Education and the Committee of Small Business.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shelby Lohr
utterances.text: My name is Shelby Lohr.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shelby Lohr
utterances.text: I'm the Senior Manager of Policy and Advocacy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shelby Lohr
utterances.text: at the Daycare Council of New York.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shelby Lohr
utterances.text: The Daycare Council of New York represents nearly 300 center-based child care providers operating approximately 13,000 publicly funded seats across New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shelby Lohr
utterances.text: Our members are both nonprofit organizations and small businesses.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shelby Lohr
utterances.text: Among other things, child care providers must meet their payroll, cover their rent and insurance,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shelby Lohr
utterances.text: purchase food and supplies, comply with extensive regulations, and recruit their staff.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shelby Lohr
utterances.text: Providers are expected to maintain a quality program, but often lack predictable revenue, timely payment, adequate rates, and reasonable control over enrollment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shelby Lohr
utterances.text: That is, child care providers are expected to operate like a business, but the public systems they depend on can sometimes prevent them from doing so.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shelby Lohr
utterances.text: These challenges are reflected in our September 2026 brief called Voices from Daycare Council Members, and it draws on member experiences and recommendations for improving the contracted early childhood system.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shelby Lohr
utterances.text: One area is that providers struggle to operate when they're faced with late and unpredictable contract payments.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shelby Lohr
utterances.text: In 2023, Daycare Council surveyed more than 250 early care and education providers, where 64% reported that they remained unpaid for the prior month's services.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shelby Lohr
utterances.text: And among providers who were forced to bridge these gaps, 25% were able to obtain a business loan, but 26% also took out personal loans to make that work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shelby Lohr
utterances.text: And sometimes also they relied on grants, bridge loans, and other private funds to sustain their operations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shelby Lohr
utterances.text: In other words, they're borrowing money, sometimes even

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shelby Lohr
utterances.text: from personal loans and family and friends to finance services that are supported by the city contracts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shelby Lohr
utterances.text: And often this is their sole revenue sources from these contracts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shelby Lohr
utterances.text: So again, they have to absorb a lot of the late fees that come with the delays.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shelby Lohr
utterances.text: Another area is that the reimbursement rate does not reflect the cost of the service that is being purchased.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shelby Lohr
utterances.text: All right, I'll wrap it up there, but there's an extensive section that I'll send over along with some of this.

utterances.speaker: Shanel Thomas-Henry
utterances.text: Thank you all for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Thank you all so much, and you've all testified before.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I'm clear on the necessity of on-time payments.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ingrid Matias Chungata

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ingrid Matias Chungata
utterances.text: They go to New York's public schools.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ingrid Matias Chungata
utterances.text: It's higher pay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ingrid Matias Chungata
utterances.text: And we can't compete.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ingrid Matias Chungata
utterances.text: We're a 12-month program to a 10-month program.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ingrid Matias Chungata
utterances.text: There's no competition.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ingrid Matias Chungata
utterances.text: So at the end of the day, we're competing with our funders.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanita Bowen
utterances.text: And I'll add that the same way family child care educators are close with their parents, we're also close with our assistants.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanita Bowen
utterances.text: And if our assistants are waiting for pay, they're skeptical about everything.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanita Bowen
utterances.text: When they see that we can't put the payment in the portal on time and get paid on time, it affects their pay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanita Bowen
utterances.text: And then when the providers...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanita Bowen
utterances.text: You know, we're people, so, you know, we may grumble a bit about whether

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanita Bowen
utterances.text: a DOE program may not address all of the hours, extended hours, overnight care, special needs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanita Bowen
utterances.text: Like, it has to address all of that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanita Bowen
utterances.text: The assistants are paying attention.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shanita Bowen
utterances.text: So new workforce is going to be a challenge.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: You mean attracting a new workforce.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Attracting a new workforce, yeah.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Thank you, guys.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Shout out to our children.

chapters.summary: Lynn Fredericks, founder of Family Cook Productions, testifies on her nonprofit's culinary nutrition programs in early child care. She supports the bill and asks for training resources for community-based and family child care providers.
chapters.title: Lynn Fredericks testifies on Family Cook Productions

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lynn Fredericks
utterances.text: Here we go.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lynn Fredericks
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Chair Thomas Henry and Subcommittee Chair Gutierrez.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lynn Fredericks
utterances.text: My name is Lynn Fredericks, and I am the founder and the

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lynn Fredericks
utterances.text: leader at a small but national nonprofit, Family Cook Productions, that has a large footprint, including in early child care.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lynn Fredericks
utterances.text: I founded Family Cook 30 years ago after using mealtime to heal my own family life when I found myself a single mom of two little boys after a divorce.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lynn Fredericks
utterances.text: I was moved to share the learnings of how my life really transformed through this nourishing food and the mealtime and bonding together and to bring that to address the health diet related health crisis in the United States.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lynn Fredericks
utterances.text: Family Cook has developed one of the widest, over 30 years, portfolios of evidence-based culinary nutrition intervention programs and curricula impacting over 345,000 individuals in 30 states and 400 locations

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lynn Fredericks
utterances.text: through a license and training model.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lynn Fredericks
utterances.text: We provides hands-on food and skills education in partnership with New York City Public Schools and New York City Schools contracted community-based family.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lynn Fredericks
utterances.text: operated preschools and child care centers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lynn Fredericks
utterances.text: Today, we have supported 253 preschool classrooms, over 4,000 families across five boroughs with our evidence-based early childhood education program called Nibble with Willow.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lynn Fredericks
utterances.text: We enthusiastically support this

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lynn Fredericks

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lynn Fredericks
